note.text: Luke opens with a single long, carefully balanced sentence in polished literary Greek, the kind that began histories and medical treatises of the day. He admits that **many** before him have written accounts (⟦0⟧, *polloi epecheirēsan*, “many have undertaken”) and promises to write ⟦1⟧ (*akribōs kathexēs*, “carefully, in order”). Most scholars think Mark was one of those “many” accounts; on the early church's view that Matthew wrote first, Matthew would be among them. Right after this preface, Luke's Greek shifts into a Semitic, Septuagint-like style.

Where Mark begins at the Jordan, Matthew with Abraham and Luke with a temple priest, John starts before creation: ⟦0⟧ (*en archē ēn ho logos*, “in the beginning was the Word”), echoing the first words of Genesis in Greek. In ⟦1⟧ the verb is *eskēnōsen*, literally “pitched his tent among us”, recalling the tabernacle where God's glory lived in Israel's wilderness years.

The two genealogies share almost no wording; the computed overlap is only a few percent. Matthew runs **forward** from Abraham with a steady refrain, ⟦0⟧ (“Abraham fathered Isaac”). Luke runs **backward** from Jesus to “Adam, son of God” in a chain of genitives, ⟦1⟧ (“of Heli”), and names a different grandfather for Joseph. Both pause at the same point: Jesus is Joseph's son ⟦2⟧ (“as was supposed”). The two lines have long been reconciled: many read Luke's as Mary's line, and Julius Africanus (3rd century) explained the difference by levirate marriage.

Luke's narrative opens in the temple, with an elderly childless couple who deliberately echo Abraham and Sarah. The Greek here suddenly reads like the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament: clauses strung together with “and”, and Hebrew-style turns such as *egeneto* (“and it came to pass”). Many scholars think Luke deliberately imitated biblical style so that the story of Jesus begins as a continuation of Israel's scriptures. This material is found only in Luke.

Gabriel's greeting ⟦0⟧ (*chaire kecharitōmenē*) is a pun in Greek: *chaire*, the ordinary word for “hello” (literally “rejoice”), shares its root with *charis*, “grace/favor”. The second word is a perfect participle meaning “one who has been favored”. Luke tells the story from Mary's side, where Matthew's birth story is told from Joseph's. The two accounts share almost no wording.

Mary's song is woven almost entirely from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2. Its first word, ⟦0⟧ (*megalynei*, “magnifies”), gives it its Latin name. Its central theme, God lowering the powerful and lifting the lowly, recurs throughout Luke: the poor, women and outsiders get more attention in this Gospel than in any other.

Zechariah's hymn (the *Benedictus*) closes the birth of John the Baptist with Israel-centered hopes: deliverance from enemies, covenant, the oath to Abraham. Luke builds his first two chapters in **pairs**: two annunciations, two births, two hymns, John always the forerunner and Jesus the greater. None of this appears in any other Gospel, and the Greek is again heavily Septuagint-flavored.

Matthew tells the birth through Joseph's dreams and introduces his signature device, the “fulfillment formula”: ⟦0⟧ (“to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet”). He quotes Isaiah 7:14 from the Greek Septuagint, whose ⟦1⟧ (*hē parthenos*, “the virgin”) renders a Hebrew word (*almah*) that means “young woman”, a difference much discussed ever since. Traditional readers note that the Jewish translators of the Septuagint themselves chose *parthenos*, two centuries before Jesus.

cites.words: ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπὸ κυρίου διὰ τοῦ προφήτου

note.text: Luke anchors the birth in imperial history with a census decree of Augustus, a dating that historians find hard to square with other sources. Defenders of Luke's accuracy propose an earlier enrollment under Augustus, or read ⟦0⟧ as “before” the census of Quirinius. The famous ⟦1⟧ (*katalyma*) is the same word Luke later uses for the “guest room” of the Last Supper, so “no room in the guest room” may be closer than “no room at the inn”. The angels' title ⟦2⟧ (“a Savior, who is Christ the Lord”) uses titles that were also claimed by the emperor.

The infant Jesus is brought to the temple, where two aged prophets, Simeon and Anna, a man and a woman, recognize him. Luke often pairs male and female figures this way. Simeon's *Nunc Dimittis* adds a note that runs through Luke and Acts: salvation as “a light for revelation to the Gentiles.” Only Luke places Jesus in the Jerusalem temple as a child, and his Gospel will also end in the temple.

Only Matthew has the magi: Persian or Babylonian star-watchers, not “kings” (that tradition came later). Gentile outsiders come to worship while Jerusalem's king plots murder, previewing Matthew's ending, where the risen Jesus sends his disciples to “all nations”. Matthew again cites scripture (Micah 5:2) to locate the birth in Bethlehem.

Matthew models this story on Moses: a tyrant kills infant boys, the child escapes, and he returns when “those seeking the child's life are dead” (wording borrowed from Exodus 4:19 in the Septuagint). The quotation ⟦0⟧ (“Out of Egypt I called my son”) applies Hosea's words about Israel to Jesus, a typical move in Matthew, who presents Jesus as reliving Israel's story.

cites.words: Ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐκάλεσα τὸν υἱόν μου

note.text: The only story about Jesus between infancy and adulthood in the canonical Gospels. His first recorded words are ⟦0⟧, literally “I must be in the things of my Father”. The Greek leaves the place unspecified (“house” or “affairs”), and translations differ. Luke's ⟦1⟧ (*dei*, “it is necessary”) is a word he uses throughout for the divine plan.

cites.words: ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου δεῖ εἶναί με

note.text: Mark introduces John with a quotation he attributes to ⟦0⟧ (“in Isaiah the prophet”), but its first half actually comes from Malachi 3:1. **Both** Matthew and Luke keep the Isaiah line and drop the Malachi words here (Matthew uses them later, at 11:10). Luke also sets the scene with a formal six-part date, the fifteenth year of Tiberius, the way a Greek historian would.

A run of **24 consecutive identical Greek words** between Matthew and Luke, and over 80% agreement in all. Since Mark lacks this speech, it is a prime exhibit for “Q”, the proposed lost source of sayings; on the Farrer view, Luke copied it from Matthew. The audience differs: in Matthew John attacks ⟦0⟧ (“Pharisees and Sadducees”), in Luke the crowds.

lede.text: John the Baptist's sermon is one of the most important passages for the Synoptic problem. Matthew and Luke agree here almost word for word, more than 80% by this site's alignment, in material that Mark does not have. This is the strongest kind of evidence for the shared source scholars call Q, or, on the Farrer view, for Luke copying Matthew.

body.text:
Compare the opening: ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ (“you brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?”). The two are identical down to word order. The warning about Abraham is the same: ⟦2⟧ (“God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones”). Oral tradition rarely keeps sentences this long unchanged, so a **written** Greek source is the usual explanation.

Where they do differ, it is in a single verb: Matthew's ⟦3⟧ (“do not presume to say”) against Luke's ⟦4⟧ (“do not begin to say”).

cites.words: Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν τίς ὑπέδειξεν ὑμῖν φυγεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς
Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν τίς ὑπέδειξεν ὑμῖν φυγεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς
δύναται ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῶν λίθων τούτων ἐγεῖραι τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ

body.text: The words are the same, but the audience is not. In Matthew, John addresses ⟦0⟧ (“many of the Pharisees and Sadducees”); in Luke, ⟦1⟧ (“the crowds that came out”). Matthew turns the sermon into an attack on religious leaders, which suits his Gospel's running conflict with the Pharisees. Luke makes it a warning to everyone. Most scholars think Luke's broader audience is closer to the source, since pairing Pharisees with Sadducees is a Matthean habit (it recurs four times in chapter 16).

Luke alone adds a question-and-answer section. The crowds ask ⟦0⟧ (“what then should we do?”), and John answers concretely: ⟦1⟧ (“whoever has two tunics should share with the one who has none”). Tax collectors are told not to over-collect, and soldiers not to extort. It is classic Luke: repentance means economic justice, and the same question recurs in Acts (2:37).

cites.words: Ὁ ἔχων δύο χιτῶνας μεταδότω τῷ μὴ ἔχοντι

note.text: Only Luke has John answer practical questions from the crowds, toll collectors and soldiers: ⟦0⟧ (“What then should we do?”). The answers are about money and possessions: share a spare tunic, collect no more than you're owed, don't extort. That fits Luke's lasting interest in wealth and the poor. The same question returns, word for word, in Acts 2:37.

This unit has 27 “minor agreements”, places where Matthew and Luke agree against Mark. Most striking is that both add ⟦0⟧ (“and with fire”) to Mark's “he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit”, and both continue with the winnowing fork, which Mark lacks. Two-Source scholars see Mark and Q overlapping here; Farrer scholars see Luke following Matthew.

In Mark the heavens are ⟦0⟧ (*schizomenous*, “being torn apart”), a violent verb Mark uses again only when the temple curtain is torn at Jesus' death. Matthew and Luke both soften it to “opened”, one of the minor agreements. Mark and Luke keep the voice private, ⟦1⟧ (“**You** are my Son”); Matthew makes it a public announcement, ⟦2⟧ (“**This** is my Son”).

lede.text: That Jesus was baptized by John is among the best-attested facts about his life, partly because it was awkward. Why would the sinless Messiah undergo a baptism of repentance, administered by someone presented as his inferior? The four Gospels can be read as four increasingly careful responses to that embarrassment. Traditional readers see complementary emphases instead: each evangelist brings out a different side of why the sinless one was baptized.

body.text: Mark says it directly: Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“was baptized in the Jordan by John”). Coming up from the water, **he** sees the heavens ⟦1⟧ (“being torn open”), and the voice speaks to him alone: ⟦2⟧ (“**You** are my beloved Son”). In Mark the experience is private; nothing suggests anyone else saw or heard it. The words blend Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1.

cites.words: ἐβαπτίσθη εἰς τὸν Ἰορδάνην ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου
Σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός

body.text:
Matthew alone adds a dialogue. John tries to prevent it: ⟦0⟧ (“I need to be baptized by you”). Jesus answers ⟦1⟧ (“it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness”). These are Jesus' first words in Matthew, and they bring in Matthew's key term, righteousness.

The voice becomes public: ⟦2⟧ (“**This** is my beloved Son”). It is an announcement to bystanders, not a word to Jesus. The heavens are ⟦3⟧ (“opened”) rather than torn, a gentler verb that Luke also uses (⟦4⟧). That shared verb is a minor agreement.

cites.words: Ἐγὼ χρείαν ἔχω ὑπὸ σοῦ βαπτισθῆναι
οὕτως γὰρ πρέπον ἐστὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην
Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός

body.text: Luke's narrative is subtle. He describes John's imprisonment **before** the baptism (3:19–20), then says only ⟦0⟧ (“when Jesus had been baptized and was praying”). He never says who baptized him. The emphasis moves to prayer, a constant theme in Luke, and to physical reality: the Spirit came ⟦1⟧ (“in **bodily** form, like a dove”). Luke then gives Jesus' age, ⟦2⟧ (“about thirty years old”), a detail found nowhere else.

The Fourth Gospel never narrates the baptism. John the Baptist only testifies to what he saw: ⟦0⟧ (“I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it **remained** on him”). John's favorite verb, *menō* (“remain”, “abide”), makes the Spirit a lasting presence. The Baptist's conclusion has a significant variant: SBLGNT prints ⟦1⟧ (“the **Chosen One** of God”), supported by some early manuscripts, while most manuscripts and translations read “the Son of God”. A scribe might well have changed “Chosen One” to the familiar title, but not the reverse.

cites.words: Τεθέαμαι τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον ὡς περιστερὰν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐπ αὐτόν

note.text: Mark's version is two verses, and blunt: the Spirit ⟦0⟧ (*ekballei*, “drives out”, the verb used for exorcisms) Jesus into the wilderness. Matthew and Luke both soften this to “led” and both add a three-part dialogue with the devil, sharing much of its wording. They put the temptations in a different order: Matthew ends on a mountain, Luke at the Jerusalem temple, his Gospel's center of gravity.

Here John's first disciples come from the Baptist's circle in Judea, not from fishing boats in Galilee as in the other Gospels. John is the only evangelist to keep Aramaic titles and translate them: ⟦0⟧ (“the Messiah, which is translated Christ”), and *Kēphas* explained as *Petros*, “rock”. In John, Jesus is openly named Messiah on the first pages; in Mark it is a secret until halfway through.

cites.words: τὸν Μεσσίαν ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον χριστός

note.text: John never calls Jesus' miracles “acts of power” (*dynameis*), the Synoptic word. He calls them **signs**: ⟦0⟧ (“the beginning of the signs”). They point beyond themselves, here to abundance (about 120–180 gallons of wine). Jesus' reply to his mother, ⟦1⟧ (“my hour has not yet come”), introduces John's countdown to the “hour” of the cross.

The conversation turns on a Greek double meaning. ⟦0⟧ can mean “born **again**” or “born **from above**”; Nicodemus hears the first, Jesus means the second. John often builds dialogues on such misunderstandings. In this Gospel the narrator's voice blends into Jesus' speech, and it is unclear where Jesus stops speaking and the narrator begins, possibly before the famous ⟦1⟧.

cites.words: Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον

note.text: In the other Gospels John the Baptist is a fiery prophet of judgment. In John he is purely a **witness** who points away from himself: ⟦0⟧ (“he must increase, I must decrease”). This Gospel also has Jesus' and John's ministries running at the same time, with both baptizing, where Mark has Jesus begin only after John's arrest (Mark 1:14).

cites.words: ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι

note.text: The longest conversation Jesus has with anyone in the Gospels is with a Samaritan woman, someone a Jewish teacher would normally avoid on two counts: ⟦0⟧ (“Jews do not associate with Samaritans”). ⟦1⟧ (*hydōr zōn*) means both “running water” and “living water”, another Johannine double meaning. The scene ends with Jesus' first plain self-identification, ⟦2⟧ (“I am he, the one speaking to you”).

A Sabbath healing in Jerusalem sparks the conflict that drives the rest of John's Gospel. Jesus' defense, ⟦0⟧ (“my Father is working until now, and I am working”), is heard as a claim to be ⟦1⟧ (“making himself equal to God”). Verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, is absent from the oldest manuscripts; see the Variants page.

cites.words: Ὁ πατήρ μου ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι

note.text: A long discourse on the Son's authority to give life and to judge. John's characteristic idea is **“realized eschatology”**: eternal life is not only future but present. Whoever believes ⟦0⟧ (“*has* eternal life”, present tense) and ⟦1⟧ (“has already crossed over from death to life”, a perfect tense).

cites.words: μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν

note.text: After the feeding miracle, which all four Gospels tell, John alone adds this long discourse. Its first of John's seven “I am” sayings with a predicate, ⟦0⟧ (“I am the bread of life”), turns into strongly physical language: ⟦1⟧ (“eat the flesh”). John has no Last Supper institution of the bread and wine, and many readers see eucharistic language placed here instead.

cites.words: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς

note.text: A frank remark that the other Gospels lack: ⟦0⟧ (“not even his brothers believed in him”). Mark 3:21 has his family trying to restrain him. Jesus first says he is not going up to the festival, then goes in secret, an apparent inconsistency some early scribes eased by changing “not” (*ouk*) to “not yet” (*oupō*) in verse 8. Many commentators read “not going up” as “not now” or “not publicly, with you”, which is exactly how he then goes.

cites.words: οὐδὲ γὰρ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ ἐπίστευον εἰς αὐτόν

note.text: Jesus teaches in the temple at the autumn Feast of Tabernacles, whose rituals included water-pouring and great lamps. His sayings about living water (7:37–38) and, in the next chapter, light play on these ceremonies. The debate is a three-way argument over his origins, among the crowds, the authorities and their own guards, who come back empty-handed: ⟦0⟧ (“no one ever spoke like this man”).

This famous story is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John, and modern editions print it in double brackets. Its vocabulary also reads more like Luke than John. Some manuscripts place it after Luke 21:38. The Gospels never say what Jesus wrote: ⟦0⟧ (“with his finger he wrote on the ground”). His one line, ⟦1⟧, became proverbial.

cites.words: τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν
Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν τὸν λίθον βαλέτω

lede.text: “Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone.” The story of the woman caught in adultery is among the most loved in the Gospels, and it almost certainly wasn't part of John's Gospel originally. It is a story that circulated for centuries looking for a home in the Gospels, and its history is part of what the site's textual-variants layer is meant to show.

body.text:
The passage (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John, including P66, P75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. No Greek church father comments on it for the first thousand years. Where it does appear, it moves around: after John 7:36, after 7:44, at the end of John, and in one group of manuscripts after Luke 21:38. Its vocabulary also fits Luke better than John. The opening, ⟦0⟧ (“and each went to his own house”), reads like the end of some other story.

Yet the story is old. The third-century *Didascalia Apostolorum* refers to it, and the historian Eusebius mentions a similar story of a woman accused of many sins, which he knew from the Gospel according to the Hebrews. Most scholars conclude that it is an early, perhaps authentic, tradition about Jesus that was added to the canon late.

cites.words: Καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ

body.text: The scribes and Pharisees bring ⟦0⟧ (“a woman caught in adultery”) and cite Moses. The law required both partners to be put to death (Leviticus 20:10), and the man's absence is conspicuous. Their purpose is stated: ⟦1⟧ (“so that they might have grounds to accuse him”). If Jesus says “stone her”, he contradicts his reputation for mercy and claims a power of execution that Rome reserved for itself. If he says “release her”, he sets aside the law of Moses. It is the same kind of trap as the question about taxes to Caesar, which the Synoptics place in the same Temple setting.

Jesus' response is to stoop and write: ⟦0⟧ (“bending down, he wrote with his finger on the ground”). It is the only time the Gospels show Jesus writing, and they don't say what he wrote. Suggestions include the accusers' own sins (an idea found in some later manuscripts that add “the sins of each of them”), Jeremiah 17:13 (“those who turn away from you will be written in the earth”), or simply that he was declining to engage. The phrase “with his finger” may echo the tablets of the law, written “by the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18).

cites.words: κάτω κύψας τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν

body.text: The famous saying, ⟦0⟧ (“let the one without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her”), doesn't abolish the law; it questions the authority of the judges. The accusers leave one by one, “beginning with the elders”. The ending holds mercy and demand together: ⟦1⟧ (“neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more”). Some scholars think it was this mercy, not doubts about its history, that kept the story out of early Gospel texts. In a church that imposed strict penance for adultery, the story may have seemed too lenient.

cites.words: Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν τὸν λίθον βαλέτω
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κρίνω πορεύου καὶ μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε

note.text: The most heated confrontation in the Gospels ends with a sentence that breaks grammar on purpose: ⟦0⟧ (“before Abraham came to be, I am”). Abraham's coming into being is an aorist; Jesus' existence is a timeless present, echoing God's self-name in Exodus 3:14 (Septuagint *egō eimi*). The listeners pick up stones, the response to blasphemy.

A story about who truly sees. The blind man's parents are afraid of being made ⟦0⟧ (*aposynagōgos*, “expelled from the synagogue”), a word found nowhere before John and nowhere else in the New Testament outside John. Many scholars read it as reflecting the experience of John's own community late in the first century, projected back into Jesus' lifetime. Others point out that synagogues already had disciplinary exclusion in Jesus' day, so the threat need not be anachronistic.

⟦0⟧ uses *kalos*, which means “good” in the sense of “fine, noble, model”, rather than the moral word *agathos*. The image draws on Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's bad shepherds and promises to shepherd the flock himself. The defining act of this shepherd is the one no hired hand would do: ⟦1⟧ (“lays down his life”).

cites.words: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός

note.text: Set at Hanukkah, the festival of the temple's rededication. The climactic ⟦0⟧ (“I and the Father are one”) uses the **neuter** *hen*, “one thing”, not the masculine *heis*, “one person”. Later Christian debates about the Trinity leaned heavily on that grammatical detail.

cites.words: ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν

note.text: The seventh and greatest sign, and in John the event that triggers Jesus' death, a role the Synoptics give to the temple incident. It contains both the shortest verse in most English Bibles, ⟦0⟧ (“Jesus wept”), and one of the boldest claims, ⟦1⟧ (“I am the resurrection and the life”). Caiaphas then unknowingly prophesies that one man should die ⟦2⟧ (“for the people”).

cites.words: Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή

note.text: A short, dark note found only in John: the chief priests plan ⟦0⟧ (“to kill Lazarus too”), since he is living evidence drawing people to Jesus. The little word *kai* (“also”) carries the irony: a man raised from death is now marked for death again.

When Greeks ask to see Jesus, he answers that ⟦0⟧ (“the hour has come”), the hour that had “not yet come” at Cana. The single seed that must die to bear fruit replaces the Synoptic Gethsemane agony. John also turns “lifted up”, ⟦1⟧, into a double meaning: lifted up on the cross, and exalted in glory.

The narrator closes Jesus' public ministry by quoting Isaiah 6 on hardened hearts, a passage the Synoptics use for the parables. Then comes a startling claim: ⟦0⟧ (“Isaiah said this because he saw *his* glory”). In context “his” refers to Jesus, so the vision of the Lord on his throne in Isaiah 6 is read as a vision of Christ.

cites.words: ταῦτα εἶπεν Ἠσαΐας ὅτι εἶδεν τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ

note.text: Where the Synoptics have the bread and cup at the Last Supper, John has Jesus wash the disciples' feet, a slave's task. The lesson is explicit: ⟦0⟧ (“you also ought to wash one another's feet”). John also dates this meal **before** Passover, so that Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are being slaughtered, a well-known difference from the Synoptic chronology. Harmonizers suggest that different groups followed different calendars, or that John's “Passover” refers to the whole festival week.

cites.words: καὶ ὑμεῖς ὀφείλετε ἀλλήλων νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας

note.text: Jesus' farewell discourse, a genre with Old Testament models such as Jacob's and Moses' final speeches. It introduces the ⟦0⟧ (*paraklētos*), a legal term for someone called to your side: advocate, helper or counselor. “Another” implies that Jesus has been the first. The chapter also holds the exclusive claim ⟦1⟧.

cites.words: Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή

note.text: The vine image, ⟦0⟧ (“I am the **true** vine”), takes over a symbol the prophets used for Israel, the vineyard God planted. The key verb is *menō*, “remain, abide”, which appears ten times in seven verses (15:4–10). John uses it far more often than any other Gospel; it is one of his statistical fingerprints.

cites.words: Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή

note.text: Some readers see a seam here. At the end of chapter 14 Jesus says “Rise, let us go from here” (14:31), yet the discourse continues for three more chapters. Many scholars think the farewell speeches were expanded in stages. The traditional reading is simpler: Jesus kept teaching as they left the room and walked toward the Kidron valley (18:1). This section ends on a note of victory before the arrest: ⟦0⟧ (“I have conquered the world”), in the perfect tense, as already accomplished.

Jesus' longest prayer anywhere in the Gospels. Instead of Gethsemane's “let this cup pass”, John's Jesus prays calmly for his followers' unity: ⟦0⟧ (“that they may all be one”). Eternal life is defined here as **knowing**: ⟦1⟧ (“that they may know you, the only true God”).

cites.words: ἵνα γινώσκωσι σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν

note.text: “Doubting Thomas” delivers the highest confession of Jesus in any Gospel: ⟦0⟧ (“my Lord and my God”). That brings John full circle from ⟦1⟧ in the first verse. Jesus' reply looks beyond the story to later readers, who believe without seeing: ⟦2⟧.

cites.words: Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου
μακάριοι οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες

note.text: John states his purpose outright: ⟦0⟧ (“these things are written so that you may believe”). The manuscripts are divided between the present subjunctive *pisteuēte* (“keep on believing”) and the aorist *pisteusēte* (“come to believe”), so it is debated whether John wrote for believers or for outsiders. This sounds like a book's ending, and most scholars think chapter 21 was added later. No manuscript lacks it, and traditional readers take it as the author's own epilogue.

Three questions answer Peter's three denials. Jesus twice asks ⟦0⟧ using *agapaō*, and Peter answers with *phileō*; the third time Jesus switches to Peter's verb, ⟦1⟧. Preachers often make much of the change, but John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere, and he varies other words here too (lambs/sheep, feed/tend), so many scholars see stylistic variety rather than a coded distinction.

The closing verses shift voice: “**we** know that his testimony is true”, then “**I** suppose” (⟦0⟧). Others are vouching for the Beloved Disciple, which suggests a community or editor finished the book. The appendix corrects a rumor that this disciple would not die (⟦1⟧), perhaps because he had recently died. From Irenaeus onward, tradition has identified this disciple as John son of Zebedee, writing in old age at Ephesus.

Mark's summary of Jesus' message is compact and urgent: ⟦0⟧ (“the time is fulfilled”). Matthew changes Mark's “kingdom of **God**” to ⟦1⟧ (“kingdom of the **heavens**”), as he does almost everywhere, a reverent Jewish way of avoiding God's name. He also adds an Isaiah quotation about ⟦2⟧ (“Galilee of the Gentiles”).

Luke places this rejection at the very start of Jesus' ministry (on the traditional reading, an earlier, separate visit) and expands it into a programmatic sermon on Isaiah 61, ending in an attempt to kill him. Matthew follows Mark closely but changes two awkward details. Mark's Jesus is ⟦0⟧ (“the carpenter”), Matthew's ⟦1⟧ (“the carpenter's son”). And Mark's ⟦2⟧ (“he **could** not”) becomes ⟦3⟧ (“he **did** not”).

lede.text: Jesus returns to his hometown and is rejected. Mark and Matthew place this midway through the ministry as a short scene. Luke places it at the very beginning (traditional readers take it as an earlier, separate visit) and expands it into a programmatic sermon that ends with an attempt to kill him. Together the versions also show a careful reworking of an embarrassing line.

body.text:
Mark's townspeople ask ⟦0⟧ (“isn't this **the carpenter**, the son of Mary?”). It is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus himself is called a *tektōn*, a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Matthew changes it to ⟦1⟧ (“the carpenter's **son**”). Luke has ⟦2⟧ (“isn't this Joseph's son?”), and John ⟦3⟧.

Why change it? Early critics of Christianity, such as Celsus, mocked a manual laborer as savior, and Origen replied that no canonical Gospel calls Jesus a carpenter. Some manuscripts of Mark do indeed read “the son of the carpenter”. Calling a man “son of Mary” rather than of his father was also unusual, and some scholars think it is a deliberate slur on his birth.

cites.words: οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τέκτων ὁ υἱὸς τῆς Μαρίας

body.text: Mark says something theologically startling: ⟦0⟧ (“he **could not** do any mighty work there”), apart from healing a few sick people, and ⟦1⟧ (“he was amazed at their unbelief”). Matthew rewrites it: ⟦2⟧ (“he **did not** do many mighty works there”). Inability becomes choice, and “not any” becomes “not many”. It is a textbook example of the redaction criticism that underpins the theory of Markan priority.

cites.words: οὐκ ἐδύνατο ἐκεῖ ποιῆσαι οὐδεμίαν δύναμιν

body.text:
Luke turns the scene into Jesus' first public act. In the synagogue ⟦0⟧ (“as was his custom”), he reads Isaiah 61: ⟦1⟧ (“the Spirit of the Lord is upon me”), to bring good news to the poor and release to captives. Then he announces ⟦2⟧ (“today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing”). The rest of Luke–Acts follows this program.

The mood turns when Jesus cites Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners. The crowd tries to throw him ⟦3⟧ (“to the brow of the hill”). The proverb that all four Gospels share is phrased differently in each. Luke's is ⟦4⟧ (“no prophet is **acceptable** in his hometown”), a pun on the “acceptable year of the Lord” he has just read. John's is ⟦5⟧. Its context in John is puzzling, since Jesus is welcomed in Galilee, and commentators still debate which “homeland” John means.

note.text: Matthew copies Mark's call story almost word for word, including the memorable ⟦0⟧ (“I will make you fishers of people”). Luke replaces it with a miraculous catch of fish and a different verb, ⟦1⟧ (*zōgrōn*, “catching alive”). John tells a strikingly similar catch, but after the resurrection, with exactly ⟦2⟧ (153) fish. Traditional harmonies take Luke's catch as a later, fuller call of men who had already met Jesus, and John's as a deliberate echo of it.

lede.text: How did Peter come to follow Jesus? Mark tells it in five verses: an invitation by the lake and an immediate response. Luke turns it into a miracle story with a huge catch of fish. John has a strikingly similar miracle, but places it **after** the resurrection. The overlap raises one of the most interesting questions about how John relates to the Synoptics.

body.text: In Mark, Jesus sees Simon and Andrew ⟦0⟧ (“casting a net in the sea”) and says ⟦1⟧ (“follow me, and I will make you become fishers of people”). They respond with no explanation: ⟦2⟧ (“and immediately they left their nets and followed him”). Mark offers no psychology and no previous meeting, only the authority of Jesus' word. Matthew copies almost all of it, with 64% shared wording.

cites.words: Δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς γενέσθαι ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων
καὶ εὐθὺς ἀφέντες τὰ δίκτυα ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ

body.text:
Luke delays the call to chapter 5 and gives Peter a reason to follow. After a fruitless night, Simon says ⟦0⟧ (“Master, we worked all night and caught nothing”), but obeys, and the nets begin to break. Peter falls at Jesus' knees: ⟦1⟧ (“go away from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord”). The address changes from *Epistata* (“master”) to *Kyrie* (“Lord”).

The commission is reworded too: ⟦2⟧ (“from now on you will be catching people **alive**”). The verb *zōgreō* means to take alive, as prisoners were taken in war, rather than to catch fish for food.

cites.words: Ἐπιστάτα δι ὅλης νυκτὸς κοπιάσαντες οὐδὲν ἐλάβομεν
Ἔξελθε ἀπ ἐμοῦ ὅτι ἀνὴρ ἁμαρτωλός εἰμι κύριε
ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν

sections.heading: John 21: the same miracle, after Easter

body.text:
At the end of John, seven disciples have fished all night and caught nothing. A stranger on shore tells them to cast to the right side, and the net is so full ⟦0⟧ (“they could no longer haul it in because of the number of fish”). Peter drags the net ashore with ⟦1⟧ (“a hundred fifty-three”) fish, and ⟦2⟧ (“the net was not torn”), unlike Luke's net, which was tearing.

The shared skeleton is unmistakable: a fruitless night, a command from Jesus, a huge catch, a net under strain, and Peter at the center. Did Luke move a resurrection story back into Jesus' ministry, or did John's tradition move a ministry story forward? Scholars are divided. The traditional reading is two separate catches, the second deliberately recalling the first. The number 153 has inspired many symbolic interpretations, from Augustine's arithmetic to Jerome's claim that it was the number of known species of fish. None has won general agreement.

cites.words: οὐκέτι αὐτὸ ἑλκύσαι ἴσχυον ἀπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἰχθύων

note.text: Mark and Luke share a 26-word verbatim run here. Matthew skips the exorcism but borrows one sentence from it to close the Sermon on the Mount: ⟦0⟧ (“for he taught them as one having authority”), almost exactly Mark's words. The demon's cry ⟦1⟧ (“I know who you are, the Holy One of God”) begins Mark's pattern of demons who recognize Jesus before people do.

cites.words: ἦν γὰρ διδάσκων αὐτοὺς ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων
οἶδά σε τίς εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ

note.text: A small but telling change: in Mark, Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“raised her, taking her hand”). Matthew has him simply touch her, and then she raises herself: ⟦1⟧ (“she was raised”). The verb *egeirō* is the same one used for resurrection. Matthew also has her serve ⟦2⟧ (“him”, Jesus) instead of Mark's “them”.

Matthew turns Mark's summary into a scripture fulfillment, citing Isaiah 53:4: ⟦0⟧ (“he took our weaknesses”). Mark ends instead with secrecy: Jesus would not let the demons speak ⟦1⟧ (“because they knew him”). Luke makes explicit what they knew, ⟦2⟧ (“that he was the Christ”).

Mark has Jesus rise ⟦0⟧ (“very early, still at night”) to pray alone, a detail Matthew omits. Mark's “that is why I **came out**” (⟦1⟧) could mean “came out from the town” or “came out from God”. Luke settles the ambiguity with ⟦2⟧ (“for this I was **sent**”) and adds his favorite verb of divine necessity, *dei* (“I must”).

Matthew and Luke both add ⟦0⟧ (“Lord”) to the leper's plea, a word Mark doesn't have here (a minor agreement), and both drop Mark's report of Jesus' emotion (see the Discovery). Mark ends with an ironic reversal: the healed man spreads the news so widely that Jesus ⟦1⟧ (“could no longer openly enter a town”), becoming an outcast himself.

cites.words: μηκέτι αὐτὸν δύνασθαι φανερῶς εἰς πόλιν εἰσελθεῖν

note.text: The central saying, from “which is easier” to “to forgive sins”, is nearly identical in all three, including the awkward broken sentence where Jesus turns mid-speech to the paralytic. Copying would preserve such an anacoluthon, but independent oral retelling would probably smooth it out. Matthew and Luke agree against Mark on small details, such as ⟦0⟧ (“on a bed”) and ⟦1⟧ (“went off to his house”).

lede.text: Four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus, who forgives his sins before healing him. All three Synoptics tell the story with heavy shared wording, which makes it a classic laboratory for the Synoptic problem. It has small editorial changes in every verse and several minor agreements.

body.text:
Mark's description fits a Galilean house with a roof of beams and packed earth: they ⟦0⟧ (“unroofed the roof where he was, and having **dug through** it”). Luke adapts the scene to the kind of house his readers would picture: ⟦1⟧ (“they let him down **through the tiles**”). Some see this as a historian's mistake, others as a thoughtful translation, much as a modern preacher might say “through the ceiling”. Matthew drops the roof altogether.

The bed changes too. Mark's ⟦2⟧ was a colloquial word for a poor man's pallet, which literary writers avoided. Matthew and Luke both replace it with forms of *klinē* (“bed”): Matthew's ⟦3⟧ and Luke's ⟦4⟧. This is a minor agreement, and a typical case of the later Gospels polishing Mark's Greek.

cites.words: ἀπεστέγασαν τὴν στέγην ὅπου ἦν καὶ ἐξορύξαντες

body.text:
The surprise in all three is that Jesus answers the friends' faith with forgiveness, not healing: ⟦0⟧ (“child, your sins are forgiven”). The scribes object: ⟦1⟧ (“who can forgive sins but God alone?”). Jesus answers with a riddle: ⟦2⟧ (“which is easier?”). Saying “your sins are forgiven” is easy to claim and impossible to check; “get up and walk” can be tested. The healing that follows makes the invisible claim visible.

Matthew adds ⟦3⟧ (“take heart”), and Luke changes “child” to ⟦4⟧ (“man”).

cites.words: τίς δύναται ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός

body.text:
Matthew and Luke both report that the man ⟦0⟧ / ⟦1⟧ (“went away to his house”). Mark has Jesus command this (⟦2⟧) but narrates only that he ⟦3⟧ (“went out before them all”). It is a small minor agreement, but one of several in this unit.

The crowd's reactions differ. Mark: ⟦4⟧ (“we have never seen anything like this”). Luke: ⟦5⟧ (“we have seen paradoxical things today”), the source of the English word “paradox”. Matthew, uniquely, has the crowd glorify God ⟦6⟧ (“who had given such authority **to human beings**”). The plural seems to extend the authority to forgive to Matthew's church.

cites.words: τὸν δόντα ἐξουσίαν τοιαύτην τοῖς ἀνθρώποις

note.text: Mark and Luke call the tax collector ⟦0⟧ (“Levi son of Alphaeus”), but Matthew renames him ⟦1⟧ (“named Matthew”). This is one reason later tradition linked the apostle Matthew with this Gospel. The traditional reading is that Levi and Matthew are one man with two names, like Simon and Peter. Matthew also adds Hosea 6:6, ⟦2⟧ (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”), which he will quote again in 12:7.

Matthew changes Mark's “can the wedding guests **fast**” to ⟦0⟧ (“**mourn**”), making the connection to grief and the coming death explicit. Luke adds a closing line found only in his Gospel that cuts against the parable's point: ⟦1⟧ (“the old is good”). It may be a wry comment on why people resist the new.

Mark says David ate the sacred bread ⟦0⟧ (“when Abiathar was high priest”), but according to 1 Samuel 21 the priest was Abiathar's father, Ahimelech. Defenders of Mark note that *epi Abiathar* can mean “in the passage about Abiathar”, the way Jews cited scripture sections, or that Abiathar, later the famous high priest, was present at the time. **Both** Matthew and Luke drop the phrase. Both also omit Mark's bold ⟦1⟧ (“the Sabbath was made for humankind”). Matthew instead adds two arguments of his own, including ⟦2⟧ (“something greater than the temple is here”).

cites.words: Τὸ σάββατον διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐγένετο

note.text: Mark gives Jesus a rare emotional moment: he looks around ⟦0⟧ (“with anger, grieved”) at their hardness of heart. Luke keeps the look, ⟦1⟧, but drops the anger; Matthew drops the whole sentence. This fits a recurring pattern, in which the later Gospels soften Mark's portrayal of Jesus' emotions.

Mark's summary ends with unclean spirits shouting ⟦0⟧ (“you are the Son of God”) and Jesus silencing them. Matthew replaces this with his longest fulfillment quotation, Isaiah 42:1–4, which presents Jesus as the gentle Servant: ⟦1⟧ (“here is my servant whom I have chosen”). The shared wording here is low.

cites.words: Σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ
Ἰδοὺ ὁ παῖς μου ὃν ᾑρέτισα

note.text: Only Mark gives the Aramaic nickname ⟦0⟧ (“Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder”) for James and John. Matthew calls Simon ⟦1⟧ (“first”), a word that matches his special interest in Peter. Luke has Jesus pray all night before choosing them, and his list differs: ⟦2⟧ (“Judas son of James”) appears where Mark and Matthew have Thaddaeus.

Matthew's blessings are in the third person and spiritual: ⟦0⟧ (“the poor **in spirit**”), ⟦1⟧ (“hungering for **righteousness**”). Luke's are second person, direct and material: ⟦2⟧ (“blessed are **you** poor”), ⟦3⟧ (“you who hunger **now**”). Which is closer to the original is one of the classic questions in Gospel study. Traditional readers often see two different sermons, since an itinerant teacher would repeat his core teaching in different forms.

lede.text: Matthew and Luke both open Jesus' great sermon with blessings, almost certainly from a shared source, the hypothetical sayings collection called Q. Yet the two versions are addressed to different people and promise different things. Matthew's are mostly about spiritual dispositions; Luke's are about poverty and hunger, and they come with matching woes.

body.text:
Matthew's first beatitude is ⟦0⟧ (“blessed are the poor **in spirit**”). Luke's is ⟦1⟧ (“blessed are the poor”) with no qualification, and in the second person: ⟦2⟧ (“**yours** is the kingdom of God”).

Most scholars think Luke's shorter, direct form is closer to the source, and that Matthew added “in spirit” and “for righteousness” (⟦3⟧, “hunger and thirst for righteousness”). The poor (*anawim*) of the Psalms and Isaiah were both materially poor and humbly reliant on God, so Matthew may be bringing out a meaning already present rather than spiritualizing it away. Readers still disagree about whether Matthew's change softens Jesus or clarifies him. Many traditional readers see two different sermons, one on a mountain and one on a level place, since a travelling teacher would repeat his core teaching in different forms.

cites.words: ὑμετέρα ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ

body.text:
Luke repeats one small word: ⟦0⟧ (“blessed are you who are hungry **now**”), ⟦1⟧ (“who weep now, for you will laugh”). Then he does something Matthew does not: he adds four woes, the reverse of the four blessings. ⟦2⟧ (“woe to you who are rich, for you have received your comfort”). The verb *apechō* was a technical term on receipts: “paid in full”.

The pattern of reversal, the hungry filled and the rich sent away empty, runs through Luke from Mary's song (1:53) to the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (16:25).

cites.words: μακάριοι οἱ κλαίοντες νῦν ὅτι γελάσετε
οὐαὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις ὅτι ἀπέχετε τὴν παράκλησιν ὑμῶν

body.text: Matthew has nine blessings (or eight, plus a closing one in the second person), and Luke has four. Matthew's extra blessings, for the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart and the peacemakers, have no parallel in Luke. Several echo the Psalms (“the meek shall inherit the land”, Psalm 37:11). Luke's sermon is set ⟦0⟧ (“on a level place”), Matthew's on a mountain, and the setting matches the content. Matthew's Jesus is a new Moses giving instruction from a height; Luke's stands among the crowd.

note.text: Only Luke follows his blessings with matching curses, so that each beatitude has its mirror image: ⟦0⟧ (“woe to you who are rich”). The verb ⟦1⟧ is a commercial term for “paid in full”, used on receipts: the rich have already collected their comfort. Matthew uses the same verb for the hypocrites who ⟦2⟧.

The salt saying survives in three different settings, a good example of how individual sayings traveled. Matthew and Luke share the unusual verb ⟦0⟧ (*mōranthē*, literally “becomes foolish”), where Mark has ⟦1⟧ (“becomes saltless”). The odd word may reflect an Aramaic pun, since a similar root can mean both “tasteless” and “foolish”.

Matthew's Jesus insists that not one ⟦0⟧ (“one iota or one serif”) will pass from the Law. Iota is the smallest Greek letter, and the *keraia* (“little horn”) is the tiny stroke that distinguishes similar Hebrew letters. Luke has the same saying in a different context and phrasing, but with the same unusual word ⟦1⟧.

The first of Matthew's six “antitheses” (“you have heard… but **I** say to you”, ⟦0⟧). It contains the Aramaic insult ⟦1⟧ (*raka*, “empty-head”) left untranslated. The closing advice about settling with an accuser on the way to court also appears in Luke 12, but there it is about reading the signs of the times.

Only Matthew has this antithesis, which moves the commandment from act to intention: whoever looks ⟦0⟧ (“in order to desire her”) has already committed adultery in his heart. The verb *epithymeō* is the one the Septuagint uses in the tenth commandment, “you shall not covet”, so the saying ties the seventh commandment to the tenth.

Luke's form is absolute: divorcing and remarrying is adultery. Matthew adds an exception, ⟦0⟧ (“except on the ground of *porneia*”, sexual immorality), and adds a similar exception in his Mark-based divorce debate (19:9). Since neither Mark nor Luke has it, most scholars consider it Matthew's adaptation for his community. The traditional view is that Jesus himself spoke the exception and that Mark and Luke give the general rule without it. Paul also cites a no-divorce command from the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:10).

Only Matthew has the prohibition ⟦0⟧ (“do not swear at all”). Compare the doubled simple words ⟦1⟧ (“yes, yes; no, no”). Nearly the same saying appears in the Letter of James (5:12), which shares several echoes of the Sermon on the Mount without quoting a Gospel.

Both open with the identical command ⟦0⟧ (“love your enemies”), but the climax differs. Matthew's is ⟦1⟧ (“be **perfect/complete**, as your heavenly Father is”), Luke's ⟦2⟧ (“be **merciful**, as your Father is”). Matthew places the Golden Rule later, at 7:12, and adds ⟦3⟧, “this is the Law and the Prophets”.

cites.words: οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται

lede.text: “Love your enemies” is in both Matthew and Luke, almost word for word: ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧. Most scholars regard it as one of the sayings most securely traceable to Jesus himself. Around that shared core, Matthew and Luke build different arguments.

body.text:
Matthew frames the teaching as one of his “antitheses”, set against the law of retaliation, “an eye for an eye”. The examples are specific. ⟦0⟧ (“whoever slaps you on the **right** cheek”) is often taken to imply a backhanded slap, an insult rather than an assault. ⟦1⟧ (“whoever forces you to go one mile”) uses a Persian loanword for compulsory service, such as a Roman soldier's right to make a civilian carry his pack.

Luke has no antithesis and no forced mile. His cloak example is about robbery, not a court case: ⟦2⟧ (“from one who takes your cloak”), so the order of garments is reversed. Matthew's tunic is taken by lawsuit and the cloak given as well; Luke's thief snatches the outer garment first.

cites.words: ὅστις σε ῥαπίζει εἰς τὴν δεξιὰν σιαγόνα
ἀπὸ τοῦ αἴροντός σου τὸ ἱμάτιον

body.text: Both Gospels argue that loving only those who love you is nothing special, but each uses different words. Matthew: ⟦0⟧ (“what **reward** do you have?”), and even ⟦1⟧ (“the tax collectors”) and ⟦2⟧ (“the Gentiles”) do that. Luke: ⟦3⟧ (“what **credit** is that to you?”), and even ⟦4⟧ (“sinners”) do it. Luke's terms would be familiar to Greek readers, since *charis* (favor, credit) was the language of benefaction and reciprocity in the Greco-Roman world. Matthew's examples come from a Jewish community's boundary markers.

The climax differs strikingly. Matthew: ⟦0⟧ (“be **perfect**, as your heavenly Father is perfect”). Luke: ⟦1⟧ (“be **merciful**, as your Father is merciful”). Both echo Leviticus 19:2, “be holy, for I am holy”. *Teleios* means “complete” or “whole” more than flawless, so Matthew's demand is for undivided love that matches God's generosity to both just and unjust.

Luke places the Golden Rule here (⟦2⟧); Matthew holds it until near the end of the sermon and adds a summary: ⟦3⟧ (“for this is the Law and the Prophets”).

cites.words: Ἔσεσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι ὡς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τέλειός ἐστιν
γίνεσθε οἰκτίρμονες καθὼς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐστίν
καθὼς θέλετε ἵνα ποιῶσιν ὑμῖν οἱ ἄνθρωποι
οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται

note.text: First of three parallel warnings in Matthew (giving, prayer, fasting) built on the same pattern: don't perform piety ⟦0⟧ (“as the hypocrites do”). *Hypokritēs* originally meant a stage actor. Matthew uses the word about thirteen times, more than any other Gospel. The image ⟦1⟧ is unique to Matthew.

cites.words: μὴ γνώτω ἡ ἀριστερά σου τί ποιεῖ ἡ δεξιά σου

note.text: Matthew's version is longer and liturgical, with ⟦0⟧ (“our Father in the heavens”); Luke's starts with just ⟦1⟧ (“Father”). Matthew prays for forgiveness of ⟦2⟧ (“our **debts**”). Luke says ⟦3⟧ (“our sins”) but keeps the debt image in the second half: ⟦4⟧ (“everyone who **owes** us”). That suggests “debts” is the older wording. Luke sets the prayer on a different occasion, in answer to a disciple's request, and many traditional readers think Jesus taught it more than once.

cites.words: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς

lede.text: The best-known prayer in Christianity survives in two Gospel versions of different lengths, set in different scenes. Matthew places it in the Sermon on the Mount as a model prayer; in Luke a disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray, “as John taught his disciples”. Where the two versions differ, they show early Christian worship taking shape.

body.text:
Luke's prayer begins with one word, ⟦0⟧ (“Father”), probably the Aramaic *abba* that Jesus used in Gethsemane. Matthew's opening is fuller and more liturgical: ⟦1⟧ (“Our Father in heaven”), the way a synagogue prayer would address God. Matthew also has two petitions Luke lacks: ⟦2⟧ (“your will be done”) and ⟦3⟧ (“but deliver us from evil”, or “from the evil one”).

A common rule in textual criticism is that liturgical texts tend to grow rather than shrink. So most scholars think Luke's shorter version is closer to the original wording, and Matthew's reflects how his church prayed it. Luke, however, gives the prayer a different occasion, a disciple's request, and many traditional readers think Jesus taught it more than once. The early church manual known as the Didache (8:2) gives a version almost identical to Matthew's, with a doxology.

cites.words: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ

body.text:
Both Gospels ask for bread that is ⟦0⟧ / ⟦1⟧. The adjective *epiousios* has no secure attestation in Greek before the Gospels, and the third-century scholar Origen thought the evangelists had coined it. It might mean “daily”, “for tomorrow”, “necessary for existence”, or even “supersubstantial” (Jerome's Latin rendering in Matthew). Its presence in both Gospels is strong evidence of a shared written Greek source.

The timing differs too: Matthew asks for bread ⟦2⟧ (“today”), Luke ⟦3⟧ (“each day”), with a present-tense verb implying an ongoing need.

Matthew prays ⟦0⟧ (“forgive us our **debts**”). In Aramaic, the word for debt (*ḥôbâ*) was a common way of speaking of sin, and Matthew's literal rendering keeps it. Luke translates the idea for his readers, ⟦1⟧ (“our **sins**”), but then lets the debt image slip back in: ⟦2⟧ (“we forgive everyone **indebted** to us”). Luke's half-finished translation is a small sign that a more Semitic wording lies behind both versions.

The doxology many Christians say, “for yours is the kingdom, the power and the glory”, is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew. It was added from liturgical use, and modern critical editions don't print it.

note.text: The third of Matthew's piety warnings: when you fast, ⟦0⟧ (“anoint your head”), that is, look as you normally do. Mark and Luke record debates over **whether** Jesus' disciples fasted. Matthew alone gives instructions on **how** to fast, a sign that the practice continued in his community, as it did in the early church generally.

The closing line is almost identical in both, except for the number. Matthew uses ⟦0⟧ (“your”, singular), addressing each listener; Luke uses ⟦1⟧ (“your”, plural), addressing the group. Luke sets the saying after a command Matthew lacks: “sell your possessions and give alms”, typical of Luke's sharper teaching on wealth.

Ancient optics often treated the eye as a lamp that sends out light. A ⟦0⟧ (*haplous*) eye is literally “single” or “simple”, but in Jewish moral idiom it meant **generous**, while an “evil eye” meant stinginess. That explains why Matthew places this saying between teachings about treasure and money.

The highest agreement anywhere in the double tradition: 26 identical words in a row. Luke adds just one word, ⟦0⟧ (“household slave”). Both keep the Aramaic ⟦1⟧ (*mamōnas*, “wealth”) untranslated. Agreement this close is the kind of evidence that persuades most scholars that Matthew and Luke had a **written** common source (or that one copied the other).

Close agreement, but with telling differences. Matthew's ⟦0⟧ (“birds of the sky”) are fed by ⟦1⟧ (“your heavenly Father”); Luke's ⟦2⟧ (“ravens”, unclean birds under the Law) are fed by God. Matthew adds ⟦3⟧ (“seek **first**”) and ⟦4⟧ (“and his righteousness”); righteousness is one of his favorite words.

lede.text: The saying about birds and lilies is one of the most loved passages in the Gospels, and one of the closest matches between Matthew and Luke. Their wording overlaps by over 60%. Their small differences are the kind that reveal two editors working on the same text.

body.text: Matthew says ⟦0⟧ (“look at the **birds** of the air”); Luke says ⟦1⟧ (“consider the **ravens**”). Ravens were unclean under Leviticus 11:15, and a scavenger bird makes a sharper point: God feeds even them. Most scholars think Luke kept the original “ravens” and Matthew generalized it, though Psalm 147:9 (“he gives the beasts their food, and the young ravens that cry”) could have pulled the wording either way. Matthew's God is ⟦2⟧ (“your heavenly Father”), his favorite phrase; Luke's is simply ⟦3⟧ (“God”).

cites.words: ἐμβλέψατε εἰς τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ

body.text: Both share an unforgettable image: the lilies ⟦0⟧ (“neither toil nor spin”), yet not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of them. Then comes the grass, here today and ⟦1⟧ (“tomorrow thrown into the oven”), since dried grass was used as fuel. Matthew's address ⟦2⟧ (“you of little faith”) is one of his favorite words for the disciples; he uses it four times, Luke once.

Matthew adds two words to the climax: ⟦0⟧ (“seek **first** the kingdom and **his righteousness**”). Luke has ⟦1⟧ (“seek his kingdom”). Righteousness (*dikaiosynē*) is a key word for Matthew, seven times in his Gospel against once in Luke, so most scholars see Matthew's hand here.

Each ends differently. Matthew closes with proverbial realism: ⟦2⟧ (“each day has enough trouble of its own”). Luke closes with tenderness: ⟦3⟧ (“do not be afraid, little flock”), followed by the promise that the Father is pleased to give them the kingdom.

cites.words: ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ
ἀρκετὸν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἡ κακία αὐτῆς

note.text: The speck-and-beam saying is nearly verbatim in Matthew and Luke, a 14-word run. The comic image is built from ⟦0⟧ (*karphos*, “a speck, a bit of straw”) against ⟦1⟧ (*dokos*, “a roof beam”). Luke places it in the shorter Sermon on the Plain, together with sayings about the blind leading the blind that Matthew uses elsewhere (15:14).

A cryptic saying found only in Matthew: ⟦0⟧ (“do not give what is holy to dogs”), likely an image drawn from temple sacrifices. The Didache, an early Christian manual, applies it to keeping the Eucharist from the unbaptized. Its meaning in the Sermon itself is debated.

cites.words: Μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσίν

note.text: Matthew and Luke agree for 24 words in a row, then diverge at the punchline. Matthew's Father gives ⟦0⟧ (“good things”), but Luke's gives ⟦1⟧ (“the Holy Spirit”). Luke emphasizes the Spirit throughout his Gospel and Acts, so most scholars think “good things” is earlier and Luke has made the change. Those who hold that Jesus repeated his teaching see two genuine wordings.

Matthew contrasts two gates and two roads, ⟦0⟧ (“through the narrow **gate**”), a teaching device also found in Jewish wisdom literature. Luke has a narrow **door** of a house about to be shut: ⟦1⟧ (“**strive** to enter by the narrow door”). The verb *agōnizesthe* comes from athletic contests.

cites.words: Ἀγωνίζεσθε εἰσελθεῖν διὰ τῆς στενῆς θύρας

note.text: The same proverb with the produce shuffled. Matthew: ⟦0⟧ (grapes from thorns, figs from thistles). Luke: ⟦1⟧ (figs from thorns, grapes from brambles). Matthew aims the saying at false prophets; Luke makes it about the heart and speech.

cites.words: μήτι συλλέγουσιν ἀπὸ ἀκανθῶν σταφυλὰς ἢ ἀπὸ τριβόλων σῦκα

note.text: Luke's version is a single pointed question: ⟦0⟧ (“why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord’ and not do what I say?”). Matthew expands it into a scene of the last judgment, where some who performed miracles in Jesus' name are rejected because they did not do ⟦1⟧ (“the will of my Father”).

cites.words: Τί δέ με καλεῖτε Κύριε κύριε καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω

note.text: Both sermons end with this parable, strong evidence that Matthew's and Luke's sermons share a common framework. Matthew's builder is ⟦0⟧ (“a sensible man”) who builds on rock, which fits Palestinian wadis that flood in winter. Luke's builder ⟦1⟧ (“dug and went deep”) to lay a foundation, more like Greco-Roman construction.

The centurion's words are close in both: ⟦0⟧ (“only say the word and my servant will be healed”). But in Luke the centurion never meets Jesus; Jewish elders and then friends carry his messages. John has a similar long-distance healing of a ⟦1⟧ (“royal official”) whose **son** is ill, also at Capernaum. Matthew's *pais* can mean either “servant” or “boy”.

cites.words: ἀλλὰ μόνον εἰπὲ λόγῳ καὶ ἰαθήσεται ὁ παῖς μου

lede.text: A Roman officer asks Jesus to heal his servant from a distance, and Jesus marvels at his faith. Matthew and Luke share this story with a striking level of verbal agreement in the dialogue, yet they disagree completely about how the conversation took place. John has a related story of a royal official and his son.

body.text: The centurion's speech is nearly identical in the two Gospels: ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ (“I am not worthy to have you come under my roof”). Jesus' response matches too: ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ (“not even in Israel have I found such faith”). The centurion's words are still repeated in the Catholic Mass before Communion. This is one of the few miracle stories in Q, which was mostly a collection of sayings, and it is the dialogue that is preserved precisely.

cites.words: Κύριε οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς ἵνα μου ὑπὸ τὴν στέγην εἰσέλθῃς
οὐ γὰρ ἱκανός εἰμι ἵνα ὑπὸ τὴν στέγην μου εἰσέλθῃς
παρ οὐδενὶ τοσαύτην πίστιν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εὗρον
οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ τοσαύτην πίστιν εὗρον

sections.heading: Face to face, or through messengers?

body.text:
In Matthew the centurion comes to Jesus himself. In Luke he never meets Jesus. He first sends ⟦0⟧ (“elders of the Jews”), who vouch for him: ⟦1⟧ (“he is worthy”), ⟦2⟧ (“for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue”). Then he sends ⟦3⟧ (“friends”) to say he is **not** worthy.

Luke's version anticipates the story of Cornelius in Acts 10, a God-fearing centurion who gives alms to the Jewish people. Luke may have shaped this story to set a pattern for welcoming Gentiles: through Jewish mediation, and with humility. Augustine harmonized the two versions by noting that one acts through one's agents. Modern scholars mostly see two editorial choices.

cites.words: ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν καὶ τὴν συναγωγὴν αὐτὸς ᾠκοδόμησεν ἡμῖν

body.text: Matthew uses the story to warn his readers, adding a saying that Luke places elsewhere (13:28–29): ⟦0⟧ (“many will come from east and west”) to recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, while ⟦1⟧ (“the sons of the kingdom will be thrown out”). Gentile faith exposes insider complacency, which is one of Matthew's recurring themes.

cites.words: πολλοὶ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν καὶ δυσμῶν ἥξουσιν
οἱ δὲ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας ἐκβληθήσονται

body.text: John 4 tells of a ⟦0⟧ (“royal official”), probably in Herod Antipas' service, whose ⟦1⟧ (“son”) is ill in Capernaum. Jesus heals at a distance with a word: ⟦2⟧ (“go, your son lives”). The healing happens at the same hour, as in Matthew (⟦3⟧). Matthew's word for the patient, ⟦4⟧, can mean either “my servant” or “my boy”. Luke has ⟦5⟧ (“his slave”) and John “son”, so the ambiguous *pais* may be where the versions diverged.

note.text: Only Luke tells this raising, and he models it on Elijah raising a widow's son (1 Kings 17). The last clause, ⟦0⟧ (“he gave him to his mother”), is word for word the Septuagint of 1 Kings 17:23, and the crowd draws the conclusion: ⟦1⟧ (“a great prophet has arisen among us”). Here, too, Luke's narrator first calls Jesus simply ⟦2⟧ (“the Lord”).

Two sharp exchanges shared nearly word for word, including ⟦0⟧ (“the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”) and the shocking ⟦1⟧ (“let the dead bury their own dead”). Luke adds a third would-be follower who wants to say goodbye at home, echoing Elisha's call in 1 Kings 19, and a farming proverb: ⟦2⟧ (“putting a hand to the plow”).

cites.words: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃ
ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς

note.text: Compare the disciples' cry in each Gospel. In Mark it is a reproach: ⟦0⟧ (“Teacher, don't you **care** that we are perishing?”). Matthew turns it into a prayer: ⟦1⟧ (“**Lord**, save us”). Luke uses his own word, ⟦2⟧ (“Master, Master”), a title found only in Luke in the New Testament. Mark's sleeping Jesus has a detail the others drop: he is on ⟦3⟧ (“the cushion”).

cites.words: Διδάσκαλε οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα

lede.text: Jesus sleeps in a boat during a storm, the terrified disciples wake him, and he silences the wind. All three Synoptics tell it, and the disciples' words to Jesus change in a way that shows how each evangelist treated them.

body.text:
In Mark the disciples rebuke Jesus: ⟦0⟧ (“Teacher, don't you care that we are perishing?”). Matthew turns the complaint into a prayer, ⟦1⟧ (“**Lord, save**, we are perishing”), words that his church could use in worship. Luke softens it to a cry of alarm: ⟦2⟧ (“Master, Master, we are perishing”). Only the verb, “we are perishing”, survives all three edits, and it is the likely core of the tradition.

Mark's sleeping Jesus is also a vivid detail: ⟦3⟧ (“in the stern, asleep on **the** cushion”). Both Matthew and Luke drop the cushion, the kind of eyewitness-sounding detail that Mark often has and the others often omit.

cites.words: Διδάσκαλε οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα
ἐν τῇ πρύμνῃ ἐπὶ τὸ προσκεφάλαιον καθεύδων

body.text: Jesus speaks to the storm as if it were a demon. Mark: ⟦0⟧ (“he **rebuked** the wind and said to the sea, ‘Silence! Be muzzled!’”). The verb *phimoō* (“muzzle”) is the one Jesus used to silence an unclean spirit (1:25). In the Hebrew Bible the sea is a symbol of chaos that only God controls, and Psalm 107:29 says he “made the storm be still”. The disciples' final question, ⟦1⟧ (“who then is this?”), has only one biblical answer.

cites.words: ἐπετίμησεν τῷ ἀνέμῳ καὶ εἶπεν τῇ θαλάσσῃ Σιώπα πεφίμωσο

body.text:
The rebuke of the disciples changes in each Gospel. Mark: ⟦0⟧ (“do you **still have no** faith?”). Matthew: ⟦1⟧ (“you of **little** faith”), and he places the rebuke **before** the miracle, so that Jesus talks to his disciples while still lying in the storm. Luke: ⟦2⟧ (“**where** is your faith?”), which implies that they have faith but failed to use it.

Mark's disciples in general come off poorly, and Matthew and Luke consistently rehabilitate them. Scholars debate why Mark was so hard on them. Proposals range from a polemic against Jerusalem leaders to a pastoral message that failure is not final.

note.text: Mark's demon gives its name as ⟦0⟧ (*Legiōn*), a Latin loanword for a Roman army unit, and the swine number ⟦1⟧ (“about two thousand”). Matthew cuts Mark's twenty verses to seven, moves the scene to ⟦2⟧ (“the Gadarenes”), and doubles the demoniac to ⟦3⟧ (“two”). He doubles in the same way with blind men (9:27, 20:30). The classic harmonization, from Augustine, is that there were two men and Mark and Luke tell only of the more prominent one. Manuscripts disagree over the place name in all three Gospels.

Mark places the bleeding woman **inside** the story of Jairus's daughter, a “sandwich” technique he uses often. Mark's father says ⟦0⟧ (“my little daughter is at the point of death”). In Matthew, who compresses the story, she has ⟦1⟧ (“just died”). Mark keeps the Aramaic ⟦2⟧. Luke tones down Mark's jab that the woman ⟦3⟧ (“under many doctors”) only got worse.

Found only in Matthew, this story closely resembles his later healing of two blind men at Jericho (20:29–34, Mark's Bartimaeus): two men, the same cry ⟦0⟧ (“have mercy on us, Son of David”), and a healing by touch. Many scholars see it as a doublet that Matthew placed here so that “the blind see” has already happened when Jesus answers John the Baptist in chapter 11. Traditional readers take it as a separate healing; blind beggars calling on the Son of David need not have been rare.

Another short story found only in Matthew, and to many scholars another doublet (traditional readers see two exorcisms): it reappears, expanded, at 12:22–24, where it launches the Beelzebul controversy. Here the crowd's verdict, ⟦0⟧ (“never has anything like this been seen in Israel”), closes Matthew's section of ten miracles (chapters 8–9) that follows the Sermon on the Mount: Jesus as Messiah in word, then in deed.

cites.words: Οὐδέποτε ἐφάνη οὕτως ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ

note.text: One of the densest clusters of minor agreements (52). Mark lets the missionaries take ⟦0⟧ (“nothing **except a staff**”). Matthew and Luke **both** forbid even that: ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧. On the Two-Source view, a second, Q version of the mission overlapped Mark's. Only Matthew restricts the mission to Israel: ⟦3⟧ (“to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”).

cites.words: πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ

lede.text: Jesus sends his disciples out to preach, with strict instructions about what not to take. This is one of the most complex knots in the Synoptic problem. Mark has one mission speech; Luke has two, one to the Twelve and one to the seventy; Matthew combines everything into one long discourse. And there are more than fifty minor agreements in this unit.

body.text:
Mark lets the disciples take ⟦0⟧ (“only a staff”) and tells them to wear ⟦1⟧ (“sandals”). Matthew forbids both: ⟦2⟧ (“no sandals, no staff”). Luke forbids the staff (⟦3⟧) in the mission of the Twelve, and sandals in the mission of the seventy (⟦4⟧).

The staff is a clear minor agreement: Matthew and Luke both contradict Mark in the same way. The usual Two-Source explanation is that Q also contained a mission speech, a stricter one, and that Matthew and Luke both preferred its wording to Mark's. Luke's two missions, one following Mark and one following Q, support that idea. Farrer supporters see Luke simply following Matthew.

Matthew alone includes a startling restriction: ⟦0⟧ (“do not go among the Gentiles or enter any Samaritan town”), but go ⟦1⟧ (“to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”). Matthew, the Gospel that ends with “make disciples of all nations”, preserves this saying that the more Gentile-oriented Luke leaves out. Many scholars think it reflects an early stage of the Jesus movement that Matthew kept in order to show a progression: first to Israel, then after the resurrection to all nations.

cites.words: Εἰς ὁδὸν ἐθνῶν μὴ ἀπέλθητε καὶ εἰς πόλιν Σαμαριτῶν μὴ εἰσέλθητε
πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ

body.text:
The Q mission speech shares a memorable image: ⟦0⟧ (“I send you out as sheep among wolves”). Luke's is ⟦1⟧ (“as **lambs**”), even more vulnerable. Matthew adds a proverb found nowhere else: ⟦2⟧ (“be wise as serpents and innocent as doves”).

Matthew's justification for not carrying provisions, ⟦3⟧ (“the worker deserves his food”), is quoted in 1 Timothy 5:18, in Luke's form (“wages”), right after a citation introduced as “scripture”. It may be one of the earliest signs of Gospel sayings becoming authoritative texts.

cites.words: ἀποστέλλω ὑμᾶς ὡς πρόβατα ἐν μέσῳ λύκων
γίνεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί
ἄξιος γὰρ ὁ ἐργάτης τῆς τροφῆς αὐτοῦ

note.text: Matthew builds his mission speech partly from material that Mark (and Luke) keep for the end-times discourse (Mark 13:9–13), moving warnings about councils, floggings and governors into the first mission. Only Matthew has the puzzling promise ⟦0⟧ (“you will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes”), long debated by interpreters.

cites.words: οὐ μὴ τελέσητε τὰς πόλεις τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου

note.text: Over half the words agree, but the arithmetic differs. In Matthew ⟦0⟧ (“**two** sparrows for a penny”); in Luke ⟦1⟧ (“**five** sparrows for two pennies”), which makes the fifth bird a free extra. Matthew's sparrow does not fall “apart from your Father”; Luke's is not “forgotten before God”. Luke alone addresses the disciples as ⟦2⟧ (“my friends”).

Matthew's image is military: ⟦0⟧ (“I came not to bring peace but a **sword**”). Luke's is the abstract ⟦1⟧ (“**division**”), and he prefaces it with a saying of his own: ⟦2⟧ (“I came to cast **fire** on the earth”). Both go on to describe a household split along generational lines, echoing Micah 7:6.

cites.words: οὐκ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην ἀλλὰ μάχαιραν
Πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν

note.text: Luke's version is the harsher: anyone who does not ⟦0⟧ (“**hate** his own father”) cannot be a disciple. Matthew softens it to a comparison: whoever ⟦1⟧ (“loves father or mother **more than** me”). The Semitic idiom “love/hate” often means “prefer/put second”, so Matthew may be explaining rather than changing. Luke adds the parables of the tower-builder and the king going to war.

cites.words: ὁ φιλῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα ὑπὲρ ἐμὲ

note.text: Matthew closes his mission speech with a chain of “receiving” sayings: ⟦0⟧ (“whoever receives you receives me”). Luke has a negative counterpart (“whoever rejects you rejects me”), and John has the same idea twice (13:20). The “cup of cold water” for ⟦1⟧ (“one of these little ones”) is a saying Matthew takes from Mark 9:41.

John the Baptist, now in prison, asks ⟦0⟧ (“are you the one who is to come?”). Jesus answers with a list stitched from Isaiah 35 and 61. The list includes ⟦1⟧ (“the dead are raised”), which is not in Isaiah, but a Dead Sea Scroll (4Q521) pairs raising the dead with good news for the poor in a list of the Messiah's works. Matthew and Luke agree in over 60% of their words here.

Long, close agreement (two-thirds of the words). Then a telling divergence: wisdom is vindicated ⟦0⟧ (“by her **deeds**”) in Matthew, but ⟦1⟧ (“by all her **children**”) in Luke. Matthew's “deeds” loops back to “the deeds of the Christ” at 11:2. The obscure “violence” saying (⟦2⟧) appears in Luke in a completely different place (16:16).

Almost all of Luke's wording here is also in Matthew. The towns condemned include ⟦0⟧ (Chorazin), which is never mentioned anywhere else in the Gospels, so no miracle performed there is recorded. A small window onto how much of Jesus' activity the Gospels do **not** narrate. The comparison with the pagan cities ⟦1⟧ (“Tyre and Sidon”) is deliberately provocative.

Luke's version introduces the prayer with a uniquely emotional line: Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“rejoiced in the Holy Spirit”). Then come 27 identical words in a row. The middle saying, ⟦1⟧ (“no one knows the Son except the Father”), sounds so much like John's Gospel that scholars call it the “Johannine thunderbolt”. Only Matthew adds ⟦2⟧ (“come to me, all who labor”).

cites.words: οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
Δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες

note.text: Only Luke has this story of a woman who anoints Jesus' feet in a Pharisee's house. It resembles the anointing at Bethany that Mark, Matthew and John tell, which Luke omits. Its punchline is ambiguous: ⟦0⟧, “her many sins are forgiven, **for** she loved much”. Is her love the cause of forgiveness or the evidence of it? The parable just before suggests the evidence. The text never names her.

cites.words: ἀφέωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτῆς αἱ πολλαί ὅτι ἠγάπησεν πολύ

note.text: Only Luke records that women traveled with Jesus and funded the mission: they ⟦0⟧ (“provided for them out of their own resources”). One is ⟦1⟧ (“Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod's manager”), a link to the court of the ruler who killed John the Baptist. Joanna reappears at the empty tomb (24:10), named only by Luke.

cites.words: διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς

note.text: Another dense cluster of minor agreements (52). Mark frames the dispute with Jesus' own family deciding ⟦0⟧ (“he is out of his mind”), a line Matthew and Luke both omit. Both add a saying Mark lacks, in two versions: by ⟦1⟧ (“the **Spirit** of God”) or by ⟦2⟧ (“the **finger** of God”, echoing Exodus 8:19). Luke loves the Spirit, so most scholars think “finger” is the earlier wording.

One of the closest double-tradition passages: three-quarters of Matthew's words and almost all of Luke's are shared. The expelled spirit wanders ⟦0⟧ (“through waterless places”), the desert being a traditional home of demons, finds its old house swept and empty, and returns with seven others. Matthew applies it to ⟦1⟧ (“this evil generation”).

A two-verse scene found only in Luke. A woman calls out a blessing on Jesus' mother: ⟦0⟧ (“blessed is the womb that carried you”). Jesus redirects it with ⟦1⟧ (*menoun*), a particle that can mean “rather” or “yes, but even more”. Mary herself was earlier said to have heard God's word and kept it (1:38, 2:19), so the reply may include her rather than exclude her.

cites.words: Μακαρία ἡ κοιλία ἡ βαστάσασά σε

note.text: Matthew and Luke agree on most of the words, but they explain the “sign of Jonah” differently. In Matthew it is about **time in the grave**: ⟦0⟧ (“three days and three nights”). In Luke it is about **preaching**: Jonah was a sign ⟦1⟧ (“to the Ninevites”). Both end with ⟦2⟧ (“something greater than Jonah is here”).

lede.text: Asked for a sign, Jesus refuses, except for “the sign of Jonah”. Mark records only the refusal. Matthew and Luke share a longer version, nearly identical, but each explains the sign of Jonah differently, and the difference may reveal a source being interpreted.

body.text: Mark's version is short and absolute: ⟦0⟧ (“truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation”). The Greek copies a Hebrew oath formula, literally “if a sign will be given…”, with the curse left unspoken. Matthew and Luke agree on a qualification Mark lacks: ⟦1⟧ (“except the sign of Jonah”), and Luke's ⟦2⟧. This is a case of Mark and Q overlapping.

cites.words: ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν εἰ δοθήσεται τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον

body.text:
What is the sign? Luke: ⟦0⟧ (“as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites”), so the Son of Man will be to this generation. The sign is the preacher himself and his call to repent.

Matthew adds a specific interpretation: ⟦1⟧ (“as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster”), so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth. The sign has become the resurrection. Most scholars think Luke's version is closer to the source and Matthew's is a later Christian reading. Traditional readers hold that Jesus himself pointed to both, his preaching and his resurrection; Matthew records the demand for a sign twice (12:38, 16:1). The detail “three nights” fits awkwardly with a burial from Friday to Sunday, which suggests Matthew was quoting Jonah 1:17 rather than counting. In Jewish reckoning, though, part of a day could count as a whole “day and night”, so the phrase need not mean seventy-two hours.

cites.words: καθὼς γὰρ ἐγένετο Ἰωνᾶς τοῖς Νινευίταις σημεῖον
ὥσπερ γὰρ ἦν Ἰωνᾶς ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ τοῦ κήτους τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας

body.text:
Both close with two witnesses against “this generation”, Gentiles who responded when Israel did not. The Queen of the South came to hear Solomon; the men of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching. Each ends with ⟦0⟧ (“behold, something greater than Jonah is here”). The adjective is neuter, *pleion*, “something greater”, not “someone”. It may refer to the kingdom breaking in, not only to Jesus himself.

The two Gospels reverse the order. Matthew puts Nineveh first, linking it to his Jonah explanation, and Luke puts the Queen first, which is likely chronological (Solomon before Jonah). These small rearrangements are typical of how each evangelist edits shared material.

note.text: In Mark this scene closes a “sandwich” that opened with the family thinking Jesus mad (3:21). His family stand ⟦0⟧ (“outside”), while the insiders are those who do ⟦1⟧ (“the will of God”). Luke, who has just shown Mary as the model listener, drops the hostile framing and makes the saying a definition: ⟦2⟧ (“those who hear the word of God and do it”).

cites.words: οἱ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ἀκούοντες καὶ ποιοῦντες

note.text: Mark calls Herod Antipas ⟦0⟧ (“**King** Herod”), but Rome never gave him that title. Matthew and Luke **both** correct it to ⟦1⟧ (“the tetrarch”), the one minor agreement in this unit. Luke's Herod is puzzled rather than guilt-ridden (⟦2⟧, “who is this?”) and “sought to see him”, a wish fulfilled only at the trial (23:8).

Mark tells this in vivid, novelistic detail, his longest story without Jesus in it. His Herod is torn: he ⟦0⟧ (“listened to him gladly”). Matthew condenses it and makes Herod simply want John dead. Luke reports only the arrest (3:19–20) and skips the banquet entirely. The Jewish historian Josephus also records John's execution, but gives a political motive: Herod feared John's influence over the crowds.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Mark's scene is painterly: the crowd sits ⟦0⟧ (“party by party”) on ⟦1⟧ (“the **green** grass”, springtime) in ⟦2⟧ (“bed by bed”, like a garden). John alone has the ⟦3⟧ (“five **barley** loaves”) and a boy, recalling Elisha's feeding in 2 Kings 4:42–44, and the crowd's attempt to ⟦4⟧ (“make him king”).

lede.text: The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, told in all four Gospels. That makes it the best single test case for how John relates to the Synoptics. The story is the same, but its setting, details and meaning are told in very different ways.

body.text:
Mark begins with Jesus' motive: ⟦0⟧ (“he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd”), a phrase from Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34. The shepherd first feeds them by teaching. Then he tells the disciples ⟦1⟧ (“**you** give them something to eat”), and they reply, perhaps sarcastically, that it would cost two hundred denarii.

The actions anticipate the Last Supper: ⟦2⟧ … ⟦3⟧ (“taking … he blessed and broke the loaves and gave”). The same sequence of four actions, take, bless, break and give, recurs at the Last Supper (14:22).

cites.words: ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ἐπ αὐτοὺς ὅτι ἦσαν ὡς πρόβατα μὴ ἔχοντα ποιμένα
εὐλόγησεν καὶ κατέκλασεν τοὺς ἄρτους καὶ ἐδίδου

body.text: Mark says ⟦0⟧ (“five thousand **men**”), using the word for adult males. Luke follows (⟦1⟧). Only Matthew adds ⟦2⟧ (“besides women and children”). This might be meant to make the miracle larger, or to correct the impression that only men were present. In either case, Matthew has noticed what the source left out.

sections.heading: John: a boy, barley, and Passover
