body.text: John's version adds details found nowhere else. It is near Passover (⟦0⟧). The food comes from ⟦1⟧ (“a boy here who has five **barley** loaves”), the bread of the poor. It also recalls 2 Kings 4:42–44, where Elisha feeds a hundred men with barley loaves and there are leftovers. Jesus ⟦2⟧ (“gave thanks”), the root of the word *eucharist*, and distributes the bread himself, with no disciples in between.

cites.words: παιδάριον ὧδε ὃς ἔχει πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους

body.text:
In the Synoptics the miracle has no visible effect on the crowd. In John it causes a political crisis. The people say ⟦0⟧ (“this is truly the Prophet”), the prophet like Moses of Deuteronomy 18. Then Jesus realizes they intend ⟦1⟧ (“to seize him to make him king”) and withdraws.

John then adds a long discourse (6:25–59) that reads the miracle as a sign: Jesus is the bread of life, the true manna. John usually calls miracles *sēmeia*, “signs”, which point beyond themselves. This scene shows how he takes a shared tradition and makes it the starting point for theology.

note.text: Luke omits this story (it falls in his “great omission” of Mark 6:45–8:26). Mark's Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“meant to **pass by** them”), language of God's self-revelation to Moses and Elijah. Mark ends with the disciples' ⟦1⟧ (“hardened heart”). Matthew adds Peter walking on the water and ends with worship instead: ⟦2⟧ (“truly you are the Son of God”). John's Jesus says ⟦3⟧ (“I am”).

A short Markan summary that Matthew copies closely. The sick beg to touch even ⟦0⟧ (“the fringe of his cloak”). The *kraspedon* is likely the tassel that the Law commands Israelites to wear (Numbers 15:38–39), so Jesus is pictured as an observant Jew. The same word appears in the healing of the bleeding woman (Matthew 9:20, Luke 8:44).

Mark explains Jewish purity customs at length for readers who don't know them (⟦0⟧, “for the Pharisees and **all** the Jews…”), and translates ⟦1⟧. Matthew, writing for Jewish Christians, drops the explanation. Mark's narrator draws a radical conclusion, ⟦2⟧ (“declaring all foods clean”). Matthew omits it too, keeping the debate about hand-washing, not the food laws.

cites.words: οἱ γὰρ Φαρισαῖοι καὶ πάντες οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι

note.text: Mark calls her a Greek Syrophoenician; Matthew uses an archaic biblical label, ⟦0⟧ (“a **Canaanite** woman”), and adds ⟦1⟧ (“I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel”). In both, Jesus' ⟦2⟧ (“little dogs”) is turned back on him: ⟦3⟧ (“even the dogs under the table…”). She is the one person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus.

cites.words: Οὐκ ἀπεστάλην εἰ μὴ εἰς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ
καὶ τὰ κυνάρια ὑποκάτω τῆς τραπέζης

note.text: Mark's healing is physical and strange: fingers in the ears, spitting, touching the tongue, a sigh, and the Aramaic command ⟦0⟧ (“*Ephphatha*, that is, be opened”). Matthew and Luke both omit this story, and both also omit Mark's other healing with saliva (8:22–26). Matthew replaces it with a general summary of healings on a mountain. Perhaps they disliked techniques that looked like a folk healer's.

A second feeding, shared by Mark and Matthew only. The details differ: seven loaves, four thousand people, and ⟦0⟧ (“seven **large baskets**”, *spyris*), against twelve *kophinoi* in the first feeding. Mark keeps the two basket words distinct when Jesus later quizzes the disciples (8:19–20). Many scholars think two versions of one event. Traditional readers note that Jesus himself recalls both feedings as separate events (Mark 8:19–20, Matthew 16:9–10), and in Mark the doubling is meaningful, and the disciples still don't understand.

Mark's Jesus refuses outright: ⟦0⟧, a Hebrew oath formula meaning “no sign **shall** be given”. Matthew adds an exception, ⟦1⟧ (“except the sign of Jonah”), repeating his own earlier saying (12:39). Luke's parallel is a different saying about reading the weather: ⟦2⟧ (“why can't you read **this** time?”).

cites.words: εἰ δοθήσεται τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον
τὸν δὲ καιρὸν τοῦτον πῶς οὐκ οἴδατε δοκιμάζειν

note.text: Three Gospels, three interpretations of the “leaven”. Mark leaves it a riddle: ⟦0⟧ (“the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod”). Matthew explains it as ⟦1⟧ (“the **teaching** of Pharisees and Sadducees”). Luke says it is ⟦2⟧ (“**hypocrisy**”). Mark's scene ends with an unanswered question to the uncomprehending disciples.

cites.words: τῆς ζύμης τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ τῆς ζύμης Ἡρῴδου
τῆς διδαχῆς τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ Σαδδουκαίων

note.text: The only healing in the Gospels that takes two attempts. After the first touch the man says ⟦0⟧ (“I see people; they look like trees, walking”). Matthew and Luke both omit it. In Mark it is placed just after Jesus asks the disciples ⟦1⟧ (“having eyes, do you not see?”) and just before Peter half-sees who Jesus is: a parable in action.

cites.words: Βλέπω τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας

note.text: Matthew copies Mark closely (over 70% of his words), but notice the harvest numbers. Mark's yield climbs, ⟦0⟧ (“thirty, sixty, a hundred”). Matthew reverses it: ⟦1⟧ (“a hundred, sixty, thirty”). Luke keeps only the top figure, ⟦2⟧ (“a hundredfold”). A hundredfold was an extraordinary harvest, the kind Isaac reaped when God blessed him (Genesis 26:12).

cites.words: ἓν τριάκοντα καὶ ἓν ἑξήκοντα καὶ ἓν ἑκατόν
ὃ μὲν ἑκατὸν ὃ δὲ ἑξήκοντα ὃ δὲ τριάκοντα

note.text: Mark's wording is startling: parables are given to outsiders ⟦0⟧ (“**so that** seeing they may see and not perceive”), ⟦1⟧ (“lest they turn”). Matthew changes the purpose into a cause: ⟦2⟧ (“**because** seeing they do not see”). Matthew and Luke both make Mark's singular “mystery” plural, ⟦3⟧ (“to know the mysteries”), a minor agreement.

cites.words: ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι καὶ μὴ ἴδωσιν

note.text: Mark has Jesus scold the disciples first: ⟦0⟧ (“don't you understand this parable?”). Matthew drops the rebuke, as he usually protects the disciples. Each Gospel names the bird that steals the seed differently: Mark's ⟦1⟧, Matthew's ⟦2⟧ (“the evil one”), Luke's devil. Luke also gives the key in a single line: ⟦3⟧ (“the seed is the word of God”).

cites.words: Ὁ σπόρος ἐστὶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ

note.text: A cluster of short proverbs that Mark strings together here and Matthew scatters across his Gospel (5:15, 7:2, 10:26, 13:12). The lamp under ⟦0⟧ (*modios*, a grain-measuring bucket) uses a Latin loanword, one of several in Mark. Mark's ⟦1⟧ (“with the measure you measure it will be measured to you”) appears in the Sermon about judging in Matthew and Luke.

cites.words: ἐν ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν

note.text: The only parable found in Mark alone. The farmer sleeps and rises while the seed grows ⟦0⟧ (“he does not know how”), because ⟦1⟧ (“the earth bears fruit **by itself**”, *automatē*, the source of “automatic”). Matthew and Luke both omit it. Matthew may have replaced it with his parable of the wheat and the weeds, which also features a sleeping sower and a harvest.

Only Matthew has this parable. An enemy sows ⟦0⟧ (*zizania*, usually identified as darnel, a weed that looks like wheat until it ripens) among the grain. The master forbids weeding: ⟦1⟧ (“let both grow together until the harvest”). It speaks to a mixed community waiting for a final judgment, a recurring concern in Matthew.

cites.words: ἄφετε συναυξάνεσθαι ἀμφότερα μέχρι τοῦ θερισμοῦ

note.text: Mark says the seed is ⟦0⟧ (“the smallest of all seeds”), a proverbial claim, and that it becomes ⟦1⟧ (“the greatest of all garden plants”). Matthew and Luke **both** say it becomes a ⟦2⟧ (“tree”), one of the minor agreements. Luke's version stands closer to Matthew's than to Mark's, so Two-Source scholars think Matthew blended Mark with a Q version. The birds nesting in its branches echo Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 17.

Nearly word for word in both, including the exact quantity ⟦0⟧ (“three *sata* of flour”), roughly 40 litres, enough bread for a hundred people. Sarah bakes the same amount for angelic guests in Genesis 18:6. The woman ⟦1⟧ (“hid”) the leaven, an odd verb for baking. Leaven is usually an image of corruption in the Bible, which makes the parable even more striking.

Mark's summary adds that in private ⟦0⟧ (“he explained everything to his own disciples”). Matthew turns it into a fulfillment of ⟦1⟧ (“I will open my mouth in parables”). That is Psalm 78:2, which Matthew attributes to “the prophet”; the psalm is credited to Asaph, called a seer in 2 Chronicles 29:30. Some manuscripts even read “Isaiah the prophet”.

cites.words: Ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὸ στόμα μου

note.text: Matthew's allegorical key for his own parable: ⟦0⟧ (“the field is the world”). The finale borrows the furnace from Daniel 3 and a phrase Matthew loves: ⟦1⟧ (“weeping and gnashing of teeth”). It appears six times in Matthew and once in Luke. Its interest in final separation is typical of Matthew's Gospel.

cites.words: ὁ δὲ ἀγρός ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος
ὁ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων

note.text: Three short parables found only in Matthew. The man who finds treasure sells everything ⟦0⟧ (“out of his **joy**”). The section ends with a riddle that many readers take as the evangelist's self-portrait: ⟦1⟧ (“every scribe trained for the kingdom”) brings out of his storeroom things new and old.

cites.words: πᾶς γραμματεὺς μαθητευθεὶς τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν

note.text: Each Gospel phrases Peter's confession differently. Mark: ⟦0⟧ (“you are the Christ”). Luke: ⟦1⟧ (“God's Christ”). Matthew: ⟦2⟧ (“the Son of the living God”). Only Matthew adds the blessing on Peter, with its pun ⟦3⟧ (“you are *Petros*, and on this *petra*”). John's version: ⟦4⟧ (“the Holy One of God”).

cites.words: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος
σὺ εἶ Πέτρος καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ
σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ

lede.text: At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers. The scene is the turning point of Mark's Gospel. Each later evangelist expands Peter's answer, and Matthew adds the most consequential addition in the Synoptic tradition: the saying about the rock and the church.

body.text:
The question is almost the same in all three: ⟦0⟧ (“but who do you say that I am?”). The answer grows:

**Mark**: ⟦1⟧ (“you are the Christ”).

**Luke**: ⟦2⟧ (“the Christ of God”).

**Matthew**: ⟦3⟧ (“you are the Christ, the Son of the living God”).

Matthew's question has also changed: ⟦4⟧ (“who do people say **the Son of Man** is?”), so that Peter's answer equates the two titles.

cites.words: Ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι
Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος
Τίνα λέγουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου

body.text:
Only Matthew has Jesus' response: ⟦0⟧ (“blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah”), followed by ⟦1⟧ (“you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church”). The wordplay works in Greek (*Petros*/*petra*) and better still in Aramaic, where *kêpā* (Cephas) means “rock” for both.

The word *ekklēsia* (“church”) occurs in only two passages in all four Gospels, both in Matthew (here and 18:17). For that reason many critical scholars attribute the saying to Matthew's church rather than to Jesus. Others argue for an early Aramaic origin. Interpretations have divided Christianity: Catholic tradition sees the rock as Peter and his successors; many Protestant readers have taken it to be Peter's confession, or Christ himself.

cites.words: σὺ εἶ Πέτρος καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν

body.text:
Mark's Jesus neither praises nor rejects Peter's answer. He just ⟦0⟧ (“strictly warned them to tell no one about him”). Mark uses the same verb, *epitimaō* (“rebuke”), a few verses later when Peter rebukes Jesus, and Jesus rebukes Peter as “Satan”. Peter has the right title but the wrong idea of what it means.

John's nearest equivalent comes after the Bread of Life discourse, when many followers leave. Peter says ⟦1⟧ (“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life”) and confesses ⟦2⟧ (“you are the Holy One of God”). This is the same title a demon uses in Mark 1:24.

cites.words: ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς ἵνα μηδενὶ λέγωσιν περὶ αὐτοῦ
Κύριε πρὸς τίνα ἀπελευσόμεθα ῥήματα ζωῆς αἰωνίου ἔχεις
σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ

note.text: The turning point of Mark. Jesus says it is necessary (⟦0⟧) for the Son of Man to suffer and rise ⟦1⟧ (“**after** three days”). Matthew and Luke both change this to ⟦2⟧ (“**on the third** day”), matching the creed-like wording of 1 Corinthians 15:4. Matthew gives Peter actual words, ⟦3⟧, roughly “God forbid, Lord!” Luke omits Peter's protest and the “Satan” rebuke entirely.

Among the highest agreement anywhere in the Synoptics: nearly 80% of Matthew's words here are Mark's. Luke adds one word that turns martyrdom into a way of life: take up the cross ⟦0⟧ (“**daily**”). Mark's closing promise, that some will see ⟦1⟧ (“the kingdom come in power”), becomes in Matthew seeing ⟦2⟧ (“the Son of Man coming in his kingdom”).

cites.words: τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει
τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐρχόμενον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ

note.text: Mark and Matthew use the verb ⟦0⟧ (“was **metamorphosed**”). Luke avoids it, perhaps because it sounded like pagan myths of gods changing form, and writes ⟦1⟧ (“the appearance of his face became different”). Matthew's ⟦2⟧ recalls Moses' shining face. Only Luke reports the conversation: Moses and Elijah spoke of ⟦3⟧ (“his *exodus*”) in Jerusalem.

cites.words: τὸ εἶδος τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ ἕτερον
ἔλαμψεν τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος

note.text: Mark's Jesus answers cryptically: ⟦0⟧ (“Elijah **has** come, and they did to him whatever they wished”). He never names him. Matthew makes it explicit, as he often does: ⟦1⟧ (“then the disciples understood he meant John the Baptist”). In Matthew the disciples understand; in Mark they rarely do. Luke omits the conversation.

cites.words: Ἠλίας ἐλήλυθεν καὶ ἐποίησαν αὐτῷ ὅσα ἤθελον
τότε συνῆκαν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι περὶ Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτιστοῦ

note.text: Mark's version is twice as long and contains a famous line only he has: ⟦0⟧ (“I believe; help my **unbelief**”). Mark's Jesus says this kind comes out only ⟦1⟧ (“by prayer”). Later manuscripts add “and fasting”. Matthew blames the disciples' ⟦2⟧ (“little faith”, one of his favorite words) and describes the boy as ⟦3⟧ (“moonstruck”), the ancient term behind “lunatic”.

All three record the disciples' reaction differently. Mark: ⟦0⟧ (“they did not understand, and were afraid to ask”). Luke keeps this, but explains that the meaning ⟦1⟧ (“was concealed from them”), as if God had hidden it. Matthew replaces the incomprehension with grief: ⟦2⟧ (“they were greatly distressed”), so his disciples understand all too well.

cites.words: οἱ δὲ ἠγνόουν τὸ ῥῆμα καὶ ἐφοβοῦντο

note.text: Only Matthew has this story. Jesus pays the annual temple tax with a coin found in a fish's mouth: ⟦0⟧ (“you will find a *stater*”), a four-drachma coin, exactly the half-shekel tax for two people. After the temple's destruction in 70 CE, Rome diverted this tax to the temple of Jupiter in Rome, which may explain why Matthew's community cared about whether and why to pay it ⟦1⟧ (“so as not to offend them”).

The disciples argue about who is greatest right after the passion prediction, and in each Gospel the answer turns on a child. Mark's rule: ⟦0⟧ (“whoever wants to be first must be last of all”). Matthew sharpens it into a condition of entry: ⟦1⟧ (“unless you turn and become like children”). Luke: ⟦2⟧ (“the least among you all”) is great.

cites.words: Εἴ τις θέλει πρῶτος εἶναι ἔσται πάντων ἔσχατος
ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία
ὁ γὰρ μικρότερος ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν

note.text: The only time Mark gives John a line on his own: ⟦0⟧ (“we saw someone casting out demons in your name”). Jesus' answer, ⟦1⟧ (“whoever is not against us is for us”), seems to clash with the Q saying “whoever is not with me is against me”. Matthew, who has that saying (12:30), omits this story; Luke keeps both.

cites.words: εἴδομέν τινα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐκβάλλοντα δαιμόνια
ὃς γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν καθ ἡμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐστιν

note.text: Mark's millstone is a ⟦0⟧ (“a **donkey** millstone”), the huge upper stone turned by an animal, not the small hand mill. Luke has a different wording, ⟦1⟧, in a different context. Mark closes with Isaiah 66:24, ⟦2⟧ (“where their worm does not die”). Later manuscripts repeat this line twice more, as verses 44 and 46, which most modern Bibles now omit.

cites.words: ὅπου ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτᾷ

note.text: The same parable with two different applications. In Matthew the sheep ⟦0⟧ (“**wanders off**”), and the point is pastoral care in the church: it is not the Father's will that ⟦1⟧ (“one of these little ones be lost”). In Luke it is ⟦2⟧ (“**lost**”), and the point is heaven's joy over ⟦3⟧ (“one sinner who repents”), answering critics of Jesus' company.

lede.text: The parable of the lost sheep appears in Matthew and Luke with the same hundred sheep and the same ninety-nine left behind, but in completely different settings. In Luke it defends Jesus' welcome of sinners against his critics. In Matthew it is pastoral advice to church leaders about straying members. The same story serves two different purposes.

body.text:
Luke sets up the scene carefully: the Pharisees and scribes grumble, ⟦0⟧ (“this man welcomes sinners and eats with them”). The parable is Jesus' answer, the first of three: a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son.

Matthew places it in a sermon on community life (chapter 18), addressed to the disciples. It follows the warning not to despise ⟦1⟧ (“one of these little ones”), and the parable ends with the Father's will that none of them should be lost. In Matthew's framing, the “little ones” are vulnerable believers, and the shepherds are church leaders.

cites.words: Οὗτος ἁμαρτωλοὺς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐτοῖς

body.text:
The verbs differ. Matthew's sheep ⟦0⟧ (“goes astray”, wanders off); in Luke the man ⟦1⟧ (“has lost”) it. Matthew's shepherd searches with a conditional, ⟦2⟧ (“**if** he finds it”). Luke's goes after it ⟦3⟧ (“**until** he finds it”). Luke's version contains no doubt about the outcome.

The ninety-nine are left ⟦4⟧ (“on the hills”) in Matthew, and ⟦5⟧ (“in the wilderness”) in Luke. Either way, the shepherd takes a large risk for one sheep, and that is the point.

Luke elaborates the finding in ways that are typical of him. The shepherd puts the sheep ⟦0⟧ (“on his shoulders, rejoicing”), the image behind the earliest Christian art of the Good Shepherd, and calls friends and neighbors: ⟦1⟧ (“rejoice with me”). The moral is about repentance: ⟦2⟧ (“there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents”). That is ironic, since a sheep can't repent. The parable shows the shepherd's initiative; Luke's moral adds the language of his Gospel.

The Gospel of Thomas (saying 107) has a third version in which the lost sheep is “the largest” and the shepherd loves it more than the ninety-nine. That is an entirely different interpretation.

cites.words: χαρὰ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἔσται ἐπὶ ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι

note.text: Matthew turns a short saying into a procedure for discipline, ending ⟦0⟧ (“tell it to the church”). *Ekklēsia* appears in the Gospels only here and in 16:18. Then forgiveness without limit: ⟦1⟧ can mean “seventy-seven times” or “seventy times seven”. It is the Septuagint phrase of Lamech's boast of unlimited **revenge** (Genesis 4:24), reversed. Luke has ⟦2⟧ (“seven times a day”).

Only Matthew tells this parable, and its numbers are deliberately absurd. The first servant owes ⟦0⟧ (“ten thousand talents”). *Myrioi* is the largest Greek number word, and a talent was about 6,000 days' wages, so the debt is beyond any lifetime of work. His fellow servant owes him ⟦1⟧ (“a hundred denarii”), about three months' wages. The ratio is roughly 600,000 to one.

Luke's long “travel narrative” begins with a solemn line: Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“set his face to go to Jerusalem”). Rebuffed by a Samaritan village, James and John ask ⟦1⟧ (“do you want us to call down fire from heaven?”), as Elijah did in 2 Kings 1. Many later manuscripts add “as Elijah did” and a longer rebuke. Jesus refuses.

cites.words: τὸ πρόσωπον ἐστήρισεν τοῦ πορεύεσθαι εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ
θέλεις εἴπωμεν πῦρ καταβῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ

note.text: Only Luke has a second, larger mission. Manuscripts disagree over whether the number is seventy or seventy-two, perhaps reflecting the number of nations in Genesis 10, which also varies between the Hebrew and the Greek. On their return Jesus says ⟦0⟧ (“I watched Satan fall like lightning from heaven”), but tells them to rejoice instead that ⟦1⟧ (“your names are written in heaven”).

cites.words: Ἐθεώρουν τὸν Σατανᾶν ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεσόντα
τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγγέγραπται ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς

note.text: Only Mark quotes the opening of the Shema, ⟦0⟧ (“Hear, O Israel”), and his scribe is friendly: Jesus tells him ⟦1⟧ (“you are not far from the kingdom”). Matthew and Luke both make the questioner a ⟦2⟧ (“lawyer, testing him”), a minor agreement. Matthew adds ⟦3⟧ (“on these two commandments **hangs** the whole Law”).

cites.words: Οὐ μακρὰν εἶ ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ θεοῦ
ἐν ταύταις ταῖς δυσὶν ἐντολαῖς ὅλος ὁ νόμος κρέμαται

note.text: The lawyer asks ⟦0⟧ (“who is my neighbor?”), a question about whom to love. Jesus answers with a different question: ⟦1⟧ (“which of these three **became** a neighbor?”). The hero is a member of a despised group, and the Samaritan ⟦2⟧ (“was moved with compassion”), the same verb Luke uses of Jesus at Nain and of the prodigal's father. Only Luke tells this parable.

cites.words: τίς τούτων τῶν τριῶν πλησίον δοκεῖ σοι γεγονέναι

note.text: Mary sits at Jesus' feet, the position of a student (Paul is educated “at the feet of Gamaliel”, Acts 22:3), a role normally reserved for men. The doubled name ⟦0⟧ is affectionate, as in “Simon, Simon”. Manuscripts vary on the next words; SBLGNT reads ⟦1⟧ (“few things are needed, or only one”). John knows the same sisters with the same traits: Martha serves (John 12:2).

cites.words: ὀλίγων δέ ἐστιν χρεία ἢ ἑνός

note.text: Matthew's denunciation is a whole chapter (23); Luke sets his shorter version at a Pharisee's dinner table. With 48 minor agreements, it is another Mark–Q overlap. Matthew's ⟦0⟧ (“straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel”) may preserve an Aramaic pun (*qalmā* / *gamlā*). The tithed herbs differ: Luke has ⟦1⟧ (“mint and **rue**”), Matthew mint, dill and cumin.

cites.words: διϋλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες

note.text: Only Luke tells this parable, introduced by a warning against ⟦0⟧ (“all kinds of greed”). God's verdict is blunt: ⟦1⟧ (“Fool! This night your life is **demanded back** from you”). *Apaiteō* is a commercial verb for calling in a loan: the man's life was itself on loan. A shorter version also appears in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 63).

cites.words: Ἄφρων ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ τὴν ψυχήν σου ἀπαιτοῦσιν ἀπὸ σοῦ

note.text: With 91 minor agreements, this is the densest overlap of Mark and Q on the site. The thief saying is almost identical, except that Matthew says ⟦0⟧ (“in which **watch** of the night”) where Luke says ⟦1⟧ (“at what **hour**”). Luke's opening, ⟦2⟧ (“let your waists be belted”), echoes the Passover instruction of Exodus 12:11. Only Luke grades the punishment by how much each servant knew.

Luke alone mentions two disasters of the day that are otherwise unknown to history: Galileans ⟦0⟧ (“whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices”) and the eighteen killed when ⟦1⟧ (“the tower in Siloam”) fell. Jesus refuses to read them as punishment. The barren fig tree then gets ⟦2⟧ (“one more year”). Luke has no fig-tree cursing.

cites.words: ὧν τὸ αἷμα Πιλᾶτος ἔμιξεν μετὰ τῶν θυσιῶν αὐτῶν

note.text: Only Luke has this sabbath healing. Jesus calls the woman ⟦0⟧ (“a daughter of Abraham”), a phrase found nowhere else in the New Testament. The argument is a wordplay on “untie”: you untie your ox on the sabbath to water it, so ⟦1⟧ (“was it not necessary that she be **untied**?”) from her bondage of eighteen years. Again Luke uses *dei*, the word of divine necessity.

The words are almost identical, but the placement changes the meaning. Luke has Jesus say it on the road, before he reaches Jerusalem, so ⟦0⟧ (“you will not see me until you say ‘Blessed is he who comes’”) is fulfilled at the Palm Sunday entry. Matthew places it **after** the entry (⟦1⟧, “from now on”), so it points to the second coming. Luke also has Jesus call Herod ⟦2⟧ (“that fox”).

cites.words: οὐ μὴ ἴδητέ με ἕως ἥξει ὅτε εἴπητε Εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος

note.text: Another sabbath healing found only in Luke, at a Pharisee's dinner. The argument resembles Matthew's sheep-in-a-pit saying (12:11), but in Luke the case is ⟦0⟧ (“a **son** or an ox fallen into a well”). Some manuscripts read “a donkey or an ox”, likely a scribe's attempt to make the pairing more natural. Dropsy (fluid retention) was a stock image for insatiable greed among ancient moralists, which may explain why this healing introduces sayings about banquets.

Two pieces of table advice found only in Luke, both ending in reversal. The first ends with the maxim ⟦0⟧ (“everyone who exalts himself will be humbled”), which Luke repeats at 18:14. The second tells the host to invite ⟦1⟧ (“the poor, crippled, lame, blind”). The same four groups are brought in a few verses later in the parable of the great banquet.

Probably the same parable, told two very different ways. Luke's host is a householder whose guests make excuses, such as ⟦0⟧ (“I just got married”, a valid exemption from war in Deuteronomy 24:5). Matthew's is a ⟦1⟧ (“king”) holding his son's wedding, whose troops ⟦2⟧ (“burned their city”). Many read that as an allusion to Jerusalem in 70 CE, and so date Matthew after it. Others see a prophecy, or a stock image of a king's punishment, and many traditional readers think Jesus told two different parables. Luke's ⟦3⟧ (“compel them”) was later used by Augustine to justify coercing heretics.

lede.text: A host invites guests to a great feast; they refuse; he fills the hall with others. Matthew and Luke both tell this parable, but they share only about 15% of its wording, so low that some scholars doubt they had a common written source here. Matthew's version especially has been transformed into an allegory of history.

body.text: Luke's version is a realistic story of social insult. ⟦0⟧ (“a certain man was giving a great dinner”), and the guests ⟦1⟧ (“all alike began to make excuses”): a field, oxen, a marriage. The angry host sends his servant to bring ⟦2⟧ (“the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame”). They are the same four groups Jesus had told his own host to invite, eight verses earlier (14:13). Then there is a second sending, to the roads and hedges outside the city: ⟦3⟧ (“compel them to come in”). Augustine later used this phrase to justify coercing heretics.

cites.words: τοὺς πτωχοὺς καὶ ἀναπείρους καὶ τυφλοὺς καὶ χωλοὺς

sections.heading: Matthew: a king, a war, a burned city

body.text:
Matthew's host is ⟦0⟧ (“a king who gave a wedding feast for his son”). The invited guests do not just make excuses: some ⟦1⟧ (“killed”) the servants. The king ⟦2⟧ (“sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city”), all while the dinner is waiting.

The story has broken its own frame. Most scholars read verse 7 as an allusion to the Roman burning of Jerusalem in 70 CE, which would mean Matthew wrote after that date. Those who date Matthew earlier read it as prophecy, or as a stock image of a king punishing rebels, and many traditional readers think Jesus told two different parables. The king is God, the son is Jesus, the murdered servants are the prophets, much as in the parable of the wicked tenants just before it.

cites.words: ἀνθρώπῳ βασιλεῖ ὅστις ἐποίησεν γάμους τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ
πέμψας τὰ στρατεύματα αὐτοῦ ἀπώλεσεν τοὺς φονεῖς ἐκείνους καὶ τὴν πόλιν αὐτῶν ἐνέπρησεν

body.text:
Matthew adds a second scene with no parallel in Luke. The servants gather ⟦0⟧ (“both bad and good”), and the king finds a man ⟦1⟧ (“not wearing a wedding garment”), who is bound and thrown ⟦2⟧ (“into the outer darkness”). Matthew's church was itself a mixed body. The open invitation does not end with entry, and the final line warns the insiders: ⟦3⟧ (“many are called, but few are chosen”).

A third version survives in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 64), where the excuses are commercial and the conclusion attacks merchants. That makes it a useful independent test of what the parable's original form may have been.

cites.words: πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοὶ ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί

note.text: Luke pairs the shepherd with a woman who searches for ⟦0⟧ (one of “ten drachmas”, each about a day's wage). Then the parable of the two sons. The father, seeing the son far off, ⟦1⟧ (“was moved with compassion and **ran**”), undignified behavior for a patriarch. The refrain ⟦2⟧ (“was dead and is alive, was lost and is found”) ties the three parables together.

cites.words: νεκρὸς ἦν καὶ ἀνέζησεν ἦν ἀπολωλὼς καὶ εὑρέθη

note.text: Perhaps the most puzzling parable in the Gospels, found only in Luke. A manager about to be fired cuts his master's debtors' bills, and ⟦0⟧ (“the master praised the dishonest manager”). *Ho kyrios* may be the master in the story or Jesus himself (“the Lord”), and the Greek doesn't settle it. The moral, ⟦1⟧ (“make friends with unrighteous mammon”), has puzzled readers ever since.

cites.words: ἐπῄνεσεν ὁ κύριος τὸν οἰκονόμον τῆς ἀδικίας
ποιήσατε φίλους ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας

note.text: A short bridge passage, found only in Luke. The Pharisees, ⟦0⟧ (“being lovers of money”), ⟦1⟧ (“turned up their noses at him”): the verb comes from *myktēr*, “nostril”. Many historians think Luke's portrait of Pharisees as money-lovers is a polemical generalization, since Josephus describes them as living simply. Read more narrowly, it describes the particular Pharisees listening that day. The next parable, the rich man and Lazarus, answers them.

The only figure invented for a parable of Jesus who is given a name (Abraham, who also appears, is a figure from scripture): ⟦0⟧ (“a poor man named Lazarus”, Hebrew *Eleazar*, “God helps”). The rich man is unnamed; “Dives” is just Latin for “rich”. The ending is pointed: ⟦1⟧ (“they won't be convinced even if someone rises from the dead”). In John, a man named Lazarus **does** come back from the dead, and the authorities respond by plotting.

cites.words: οὐδ ἐάν τις ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ πεισθήσονται

note.text: Luke's mustard-seed faith uproots a tree (⟦0⟧, “this mulberry tree”) and plants it in the sea, where Matthew and Mark have faith that moves a mountain. Then a stark parable about duty, found only in Luke, ending ⟦1⟧ (“we are unworthy slaves; we have only done what we ought”). *Achreioi* literally means “useless” or “owed nothing”, that is, no special credit for doing one's job.

Only Luke tells this healing. Of ten lepers healed, one returns to give thanks, ⟦0⟧ (“and he was a **Samaritan**”). Jesus calls him ⟦1⟧ (“this foreigner”). *Allogenēs* appears nowhere else in the New Testament, but it is the word carved on the Jerusalem temple's warning inscriptions, which forbade any foreigner, on pain of death, to pass into the inner courts.

Only Luke tells this parable. The judge gives in to a persistent widow, he admits, ⟦0⟧ (“so she won't finally wear me out”). *Hypōpiazō* is a boxing term, literally “give a black eye”, which makes this one of the few comic lines in the Gospels. The argument runs from lesser to greater: if even he yields, will not God ⟦1⟧ (“vindicate his chosen ones”)?

cites.words: ἵνα μὴ εἰς τέλος ἐρχομένη ὑπωπιάζῃ με
ποιήσῃ τὴν ἐκδίκησιν τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν αὐτοῦ

note.text: The Pharisee prays ⟦0⟧ (“to/about himself”), ambiguous in Greek. The tax collector prays ⟦1⟧ (“God, be merciful to me, **the** sinner”). The verb is the language of atonement sacrifice, and the article makes him *the* sinner par excellence. He went home ⟦2⟧ (“justified”), one of the few places a Gospel uses Paul's key word in Paul's sense.

cites.words: Ὁ θεός ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ

note.text: Mark's Jesus adds ⟦0⟧ (“and if **she** divorces her husband…”), which reflects Roman law, where a wife could initiate divorce, more than Jewish practice. Yet the saying had a target close at hand: Herodias, a Jewish princess, had left her husband to marry Herod Antipas. Matthew drops that line and inserts his exception, ⟦1⟧ (“except for sexual immorality”), as he did in the Sermon. He alone adds the enigmatic saying about those who become ⟦2⟧ (“eunuchs”) for the kingdom's sake.

cites.words: καὶ ἐὰν αὐτὴ ἀπολύσασα τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς

note.text: Mark says that when the disciples turned the children away, Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“was **indignant**”). Matthew and Luke both omit his anger, part of the pattern of softening Jesus' emotions. Luke makes the children ⟦1⟧ (“babies”). Matthew omits Mark's saying about receiving the kingdom ⟦2⟧ (“like a child”) here, because he used it already at 18:3. Mark and Luke share 29 words in a row.

A famous theological edit. In Mark the man calls Jesus “good teacher” and Jesus objects: ⟦0⟧ (“why do you call **me** good? No one is good but God alone”). Matthew rewrites both question and answer: ⟦1⟧ (“why do you ask me about **what is good**?”). Only Mark says Jesus, looking at him, ⟦2⟧ (“loved him”). He is “young” only in Matthew and a “ruler” only in Luke.

cites.words: Τί με λέγεις ἀγαθόν οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός
Τί με ἐρωτᾷς περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ

lede.text: A man asks Jesus how to gain eternal life, is told to sell everything, and goes away grieving. “The rich young ruler” is a composite: only Matthew calls him young, only Luke calls him a ruler, and all three agree he was rich. The opening exchange also contains one of the best-known theological edits in the Gospels.

body.text:
In Mark the man kneels and says ⟦0⟧ (“Good Teacher”), and Jesus replies ⟦1⟧ (“why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone”). Luke keeps this word for word (⟦2⟧).

Matthew moves the adjective. The man asks ⟦3⟧ (“Teacher, what **good thing** must I do?”), and Jesus says ⟦4⟧ (“why do you ask me **about the good**?”). The change removes any implication that Jesus disclaimed being good. This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for Markan priority. It is easy to see why Matthew would soften Mark's version, and very hard to see why Mark would make Matthew's version more awkward.

cites.words: Τί με λέγεις ἀγαθόν οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός
Τί με ἐρωτᾷς περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ

sections.heading: Love, and the one thing lacking

body.text:
Only Mark says that Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“looked at him and loved him”). It is the only time in the Synoptics that Jesus is said to love a specific individual, and both Matthew and Luke leave it out. Then: ⟦1⟧ (“you lack one thing”).

Matthew moves the lack into the man's own mouth: ⟦2⟧ (“what do I still lack?”). Only Matthew calls him a ⟦3⟧ (“young man”), and adds a condition: ⟦4⟧ (“if you wish to be **perfect**”). Later Christian ethics built on this phrase a two-level distinction between commandments for everyone and “counsels of perfection” for monks, a reading many interpreters think goes beyond Matthew's intention.

The man leaves grieving, ⟦0⟧ (“for he had many possessions”). Matthew copies the phrase exactly (⟦1⟧); Luke heightens it: ⟦2⟧ (“for he was **extremely** rich”). Luke also calls him ⟦3⟧ (“a ruler”).

Jesus' image of a ⟦4⟧ (“camel through the eye of a needle”) has attracted softening explanations: a supposed “Needle Gate” in Jerusalem (there is no evidence for one), or a misreading of *kamēlos* (camel) as *kamilos* (rope), a reading found in some late manuscripts. Rabbinic texts use an elephant through a needle's eye as a proverb for the impossible. The exaggeration is deliberate, and the answer is ⟦5⟧ (“for all things are possible with God”).

cites.words: κάμηλον διὰ τῆς τρυμαλιᾶς τῆς ῥαφίδος
πάντα γὰρ δυνατὰ παρὰ τῷ θεῷ

note.text: Only Matthew tells this parable: everyone receives a full day's wage, from the dawn workers to those hired an hour before sunset. The owner's question is literally ⟦0⟧ (“or is your eye **evil** because I am **good**?”). The “evil eye” is the Jewish idiom for envy and stinginess (see the sound-eye saying in 6:23). It ends ⟦1⟧ (“the last will be first”).

cites.words: ἢ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός ἐστιν ὅτι ἐγὼ ἀγαθός εἰμι

note.text: The most detailed of the three predictions, almost a summary of the Passion narrative. Mark's scene is eerie: Jesus walks ahead ⟦0⟧ (“and they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid”). Mark says they will ⟦1⟧ (“kill”) him. Matthew is the first to make the method explicit, ⟦2⟧ (“crucify”). Luke stresses incomprehension: ⟦3⟧ (“this saying was hidden from them”).

cites.words: καὶ ἐθαμβοῦντο οἱ δὲ ἀκολουθοῦντες ἐφοβοῦντο
ἦν τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο κεκρυμμένον ἀπ αὐτῶν

note.text: In Mark, James and John ask for the best seats themselves. Matthew has ⟦0⟧ (“the mother of the sons of Zebedee”) ask, taking some of the embarrassment off the apostles. Mark's climax is one of the few places Jesus explains his death: ⟦1⟧ (“to give his life as a **ransom** for many”). Luke moves the dispute to the Last Supper and drops the ransom: ⟦2⟧ (“I am among you as one who serves”).

cites.words: δοῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν
ἐγὼ δὲ ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν εἰμι ὡς ὁ διακονῶν

note.text: Mark names the beggar, ⟦0⟧ (“the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus”), translating the Aramaic *bar* (“son of”) in advance. He is the only person Jesus heals in Mark who is named. Matthew doubles him, ⟦1⟧ (“two blind men”), as with the Gerasene. Only Mark has the vivid gesture ⟦2⟧ (“throwing off his cloak”). Luke has the healing happen as Jesus **approaches** Jericho, where Mark has him leaving it. A traditional solution: there were two Jerichos, the old town and Herod's new one, a short walk apart.

Only Luke tells this story. Jesus says ⟦0⟧ (“**today** I **must** stay at your house”), using two of Luke's favorite words. Zacchaeus promises to repay ⟦1⟧ (“fourfold”), the penalty in Exodus 22:1 for a stolen sheep, well beyond what the Law required for fraud. The closing line, ⟦2⟧ (“to seek and save the lost”), echoes God as shepherd in Ezekiel 34:16.

cites.words: σήμερον γὰρ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σου δεῖ με μεῖναι

note.text: Same skeleton, different numbers. Matthew's master gives ⟦0⟧ (“five talents”), two, and one, each about twenty years' wages. Luke's nobleman gives ⟦1⟧ (“ten minas”) to ten servants, one each, a mina being 1/60 of a talent. Luke weaves in a second plot: citizens who send a delegation saying ⟦2⟧ (“we don't want this man to rule over us”). This closely matches what happened when Herod's son Archelaus went to Rome in 4 BCE.

cites.words: Οὐ θέλομεν τοῦτον βασιλεῦσαι ἐφ ἡμᾶς

lede.text: A master entrusts money to his servants, goes away, and returns to settle accounts. Matthew and Luke tell versions of the same parable that share its plot, its final proverb and the excuse of the fearful servant, but differ in nearly every number. Luke has also woven in a second, darker story about a king.

body.text:
Matthew's master gives ⟦0⟧ to one servant, two to another and one to a third, ⟦1⟧ (“each according to his ability”). A talent was roughly fifteen to twenty years' wages, so these are vast sums. Luke's nobleman gives ⟦2⟧ (“ten servants”) one mina each, about three months' wages, with the instruction ⟦3⟧ (“do business until I come”). Only three of the ten are ever accounted for, a sign, on the usual reading, that Luke has adapted a three-servant story. Traditional readers often see two different parables with a common shape, told on different occasions.

The English word “talent”, meaning a natural gift, comes from this parable, through medieval allegorical readings of Matthew's version.

The third servant's excuse is nearly identical in both: the master reaps where he did not sow. Matthew's servant calls him ⟦0⟧ (“hard”); Luke's calls him ⟦1⟧ (“severe”), and adds a banking image: ⟦2⟧ (“you withdraw what you did not deposit”).

Both end with the same unsettling proverb: ⟦3⟧ (“to everyone who has, more will be given”), and ⟦4⟧. Mark has a version of the same saying in a different context (4:25), so it may have circulated on its own before being attached to this parable.

Luke's master is ⟦0⟧ (“a nobleman”) who goes to a distant country ⟦1⟧ (“to receive a kingdom”). His citizens send a delegation after him: ⟦2⟧ (“we do not want this man to rule over us”). In 4 BCE, Herod's son Archelaus did exactly that, traveling to Rome to be confirmed as king while a Jewish delegation went to oppose him. Luke's audience may have recognized the history.

The story ends with the king ordering ⟦3⟧ (“slaughter them in front of me”). Luke places the parable just before Jesus enters Jerusalem, to correct those who thought ⟦4⟧ (“the kingdom of God was about to appear immediately”). Matthew's rewards are joy (⟦5⟧); Luke's are political: ⟦6⟧ (“authority over ten cities”).

cites.words: Οὐ θέλομεν τοῦτον βασιλεῦσαι ἐφ ἡμᾶς
παραχρῆμα μέλλει ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναφαίνεσθαι
εἴσελθε εἰς τὴν χαρὰν τοῦ κυρίου σου

note.text: Mark's chief priests resolve ⟦0⟧ (“not during the festival”), yet the arrest happens during the festival anyway, an irony Mark leaves unspoken. John gives the plot a political motive: ⟦1⟧ (“the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation”). Caiaphas then says more than he knows: ⟦2⟧ (“that one man should die for the people”).

cites.words: ἐλεύσονται οἱ Ῥωμαῖοι καὶ ἀροῦσιν ἡμῶν καὶ τὸν τόπον καὶ τὸ ἔθνος
ἵνα εἷς ἄνθρωπος ἀποθάνῃ ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ

note.text: A rare, striking verbal link between Mark and John: both describe the ointment with the same unusual phrase, ⟦0⟧ (“ointment of *pistic* nard”) and ⟦1⟧. *Pistikēs* appears nowhere else in Greek of the time; it may mean “genuine” or derive from the pistachio. Both also price it at ⟦2⟧ (“three hundred denarii”). Mark's woman is anonymous, though Jesus promises ⟦3⟧ (“in memory of her”). John names her Mary.

lede.text: A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus. The story is told four times, and the versions overlap in a tangle that has puzzled readers since antiquity. Mark and Matthew have an unnamed woman anointing his head in Bethany; John has Mary of Bethany anointing his feet; Luke has a forgiven sinner in Galilee. Is it one event, two, or three?

sections.heading: Mark: a woman to be remembered

body.text:
In Mark the woman is unnamed. She breaks an ⟦0⟧ (“alabaster flask of very costly ointment of pure nard”) and pours it on Jesus' **head**, the way kings were anointed in the Old Testament. Onlookers complain that it could have been sold for ⟦1⟧ (“more than three hundred denarii”), about a year's wages for a laborer.

Jesus reinterprets her act: ⟦2⟧ (“she has anointed my body beforehand for burial”). He then makes a promise found in no other story: ⟦3⟧ (“what she has done will be told in memory of her”). The irony, often noted by feminist scholars, is that her name was not preserved.

cites.words: προέλαβεν μυρίσαι τὸ σῶμά μου εἰς τὸν ἐνταφιασμόν
ὃ ἐποίησεν αὕτη λαληθήσεται εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς

body.text: Matthew follows Mark closely; the alignment shows about 60% shared wording. He sharpens one detail: Mark's vague ⟦0⟧ (“some”) become ⟦1⟧ (“the disciples”). This is unusual, because Matthew more often softens Mark's criticism of the Twelve.

sections.heading: John: Mary, the feet, and Judas

body.text:
John's version has strikingly specific links to Mark: the same rare phrase ⟦0⟧, and the same sum, ⟦1⟧. The adjective *pistikos*, probably “genuine” or “pure”, is almost unknown in Greek outside these two passages, which makes independent use by both writers unlikely.

Yet John's woman is Mary, sister of Lazarus, and she anoints the **feet** and ⟦2⟧ (“wiped them with her hair”). That gesture belongs to Luke's quite different story of a sinful woman, who ⟦3⟧ (“wiped them with the hair of her head”). The complainer in John is named: ⟦4⟧, whom John alone calls a thief who ⟦5⟧ (“used to take what was put in” the common purse).

cites.words: ταῖς θριξὶν τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτῆς ἐξέμασσεν

body.text:
The most common scholarly explanation is that oral tradition blended two stories: a Bethany anointing on the head before the Passion, and a Galilean sinful woman weeping on Jesus' feet. John's version shows features of both. Many traditional readers keep the events apart: a sinful woman in Galilee earlier in the ministry, and Mary of Bethany days before the Passion, with Mark and Matthew placing the Bethany meal just before the betrayal for thematic reasons.

Later Western tradition went further. Pope Gregory the Great (591 CE) identified the sinful woman of Luke 7 with Mary of Bethany and with Mary Magdalene, producing the penitent-prostitute Magdalene of Western art. No Gospel makes that link. The Catholic Church quietly set the identification aside in its 1969 liturgical calendar.

note.text: Mark has one animal, a ⟦0⟧ (“colt”). Matthew has two, ⟦1⟧ (“a donkey and a colt with her”), which many scholars think comes from reading Zechariah 9:9's poetic parallelism literally (traditional readers answer that the colt was brought with its mother): ⟦2⟧ (“on a donkey **and** on a colt”). Only John mentions ⟦3⟧ (“palm branches”). Luke drops the Hebrew “Hosanna” and echoes the angels at the nativity: ⟦4⟧ (“peace in heaven and glory in the highest”).

cites.words: ὄνον δεδεμένην καὶ πῶλον μετ αὐτῆς
ἐν οὐρανῷ εἰρήνη καὶ δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις

lede.text: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey in all four Gospels, a rare case in which John and the Synoptics clearly tell the same event. How many animals there were, what the crowd shouted, and who understood what was happening differ from Gospel to Gospel, and the differences show each writer's method.

body.text:
Mark has one ⟦0⟧ (“colt”), and Jesus sits on it. Matthew has the disciples find ⟦1⟧ (“a donkey tied, and a colt with her”) and says Jesus ⟦2⟧ (“sat on them”). The reason is the prophecy Matthew quotes, Zechariah 9:9: ⟦3⟧ (“on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey”).

Hebrew poetry often says the same thing twice in parallel lines; Zechariah means one animal. On the critical reading, Matthew takes the lines literally and adds a second donkey. Critics see Matthew shaping the story to fit the text; defenders note that an unbroken colt might well be brought with its mother. Either way, the change follows from the prophecy he cites, ⟦4⟧ (“so that what was spoken might be fulfilled”).

cites.words: ὄνον δεδεμένην καὶ πῶλον μετ αὐτῆς
ἐπὶ ὄνον καὶ ἐπὶ πῶλον υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου

body.text:
All four Gospels quote Psalm 118:26, ⟦0⟧ (“blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”), but each adds a different interpretation:

**Mark**: ⟦1⟧ (“blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David”).

**Luke**: puts the king inside the psalm verse, ⟦2⟧ (“the **king** who comes”), and drops the Aramaic *Hosanna*, which his Gentile readers would not know. He adds ⟦3⟧ (“peace in heaven”), echoing the angels' song at the birth (2:14).

**John**: ⟦4⟧ (“the King of Israel”), and only John mentions ⟦5⟧ (“palm branches”), which is where Palm Sunday gets its name.

cites.words: Εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου
Εὐλογημένη ἡ ἐρχομένη βασιλεία τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Δαυίδ

body.text:
Luke adds a short exchange. Some Pharisees ask Jesus to rebuke his disciples, and he answers ⟦0⟧ (“if these are silent, the stones will cry out”). This may echo Habakkuk 2:11.

John adds a comment that is valuable for understanding how the Gospels were written: ⟦1⟧ (“his disciples did not understand these things at first”). Only after Jesus was glorified did they remember the scriptures. John admits openly what scholars infer about all four Gospels: the events were understood, and narrated, in light of the resurrection.

cites.words: ἐὰν οὗτοι σιωπήσουσιν οἱ λίθοι κράξουσιν
ταῦτα οὐκ ἔγνωσαν αὐτοῦ οἱ μαθηταὶ τὸ πρῶτον

note.text: Only Luke has Jesus weep over the city as he approaches: ⟦0⟧ (“if only you had known on this day the things that make for peace”). It is a pun, since Jerusalem was popularly etymologized as “city of peace”. The oracle describes a siege, embankment and all, and ends ⟦1⟧ (“you did not recognize the time of your **visitation**”), echoing 1:68 and 7:16.

cites.words: Εἰ ἔγνως ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ καὶ σὺ τὰ πρὸς εἰρήνην
οὐκ ἔγνως τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς σου

note.text: Mark adds a puzzling remark: Jesus found nothing but leaves, ⟦0⟧ (“for it was not the season for figs”). Why curse a tree for being out of season? The answer seems to be symbolic: Mark wraps the temple scene between the cursing and the withering, so the tree stands for the temple. Matthew drops the awkward remark and has the tree wither ⟦1⟧ (“at once”), dissolving Mark's sandwich.

cites.words: ὁ γὰρ καιρὸς οὐκ ἦν σύκων

note.text: The Synoptics place this at the end of Jesus' ministry, as the trigger for his arrest; John places it at the beginning (chapter 2). The traditional view is that Jesus cleared the temple twice. Mark quotes Isaiah 56:7 in full: ⟦0⟧ (“a house of prayer **for all the nations**”). Matthew and Luke both drop “for all the nations”. John's Jesus objects to ⟦1⟧ (“a house of trade”) and says ⟦2⟧ (“destroy this temple”), a saying the Synoptics place in the mouths of false witnesses.

cites.words: οἶκος προσευχῆς κληθήσεται πᾶσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν

lede.text: Jesus overturning tables in the Temple is in all four Gospels, but John places it at the **start** of Jesus' ministry, and the Synoptics in his last week. It is the largest chronological disagreement between John and the Synoptics, and how one explains it shows how one thinks the Gospels work.

body.text:
In Mark, Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“began to drive out those selling and buying”) and overturns the tables of the money changers. Only Mark adds ⟦1⟧ (“he would not let anyone carry a vessel through the temple”), in effect halting the Temple's daily business. Matthew and Luke both drop this verse, perhaps because it seemed implausible or too disruptive.

John's version is the most violent: Jesus makes ⟦2⟧ (“a whip of cords”), drives out the sheep and cattle, and ⟦3⟧ (“poured out the coins”).

cites.words: ἤρξατο ἐκβάλλειν τοὺς πωλοῦντας καὶ τοὺς ἀγοράζοντας
οὐκ ἤφιεν ἵνα τις διενέγκῃ σκεῦος διὰ τοῦ ἱεροῦ

body.text:
Mark quotes Isaiah 56:7 in full: ⟦0⟧ (“my house shall be called a house of prayer **for all the nations**”). The trading probably took place in the Court of the Gentiles, the only part of the Temple open to non-Jews, so the phrase matters. Matthew (⟦1⟧) and Luke (⟦2⟧) both omit “for all the nations”. This is a minor agreement of omission. A common explanation is that both wrote after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE, when the promise about the Temple's future no longer made sense. Those who date Matthew and Luke earlier see a simple abbreviation.

John uses different words altogether: ⟦3⟧ (“do not make my Father's house a house of trade”), which echoes Zechariah 14:21 rather than Isaiah.

cites.words: Ὁ οἶκός μου οἶκος προσευχῆς κληθήσεται πᾶσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν
μὴ ποιεῖτε τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου οἶκον ἐμπορίου

body.text:
In John, the Temple action leads to a riddle: ⟦0⟧ (“destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”), which the narrator explains: ⟦1⟧ (“he was speaking of the temple of his body”). In Mark, a garbled version of the same saying comes up at the trial (14:58), from false witnesses.

There are three main explanations. Traditional harmonizers propose two cleansings, one early and one late. Most critical scholars think there was one, which the Synoptics placed late because their structure has only one trip to Jerusalem, and which John moved to the start as a theological overture. A minority argue that John's dating is historically more likely. The data on this site can't settle the question, but it shows how little wording the two accounts share.

cites.words: Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν
ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔλεγεν περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ

note.text: Peter notices the next morning: ⟦0⟧ (“the fig tree you cursed has withered”). The lesson that follows is about faith that can say ⟦1⟧ (“to **this** mountain, be lifted up”), perhaps the Temple Mount itself. Mark adds a saying on forgiveness that echoes the Lord's Prayer, which his Gospel otherwise lacks: ⟦2⟧ (“your Father in heaven”). Later manuscripts add verse 26.

cites.words: ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς

note.text: Among the most closely copied debates in the triple tradition: around 70% of Matthew's words are Mark's. Jesus answers with a counter-question: ⟦0⟧ (“John's baptism: from heaven or from humans?”). “Heaven” is a reverent substitute for “God”. Five small minor agreements, such as both Matthew and Luke adding that Jesus was **teaching** in the temple, show the later evangelists editing together.

cites.words: τὸ βάπτισμα τὸ Ἰωάννου ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἦν ἢ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων

note.text: Only Matthew has this parable: one son says no but goes to work, the other says yes but doesn't go. The verdict: ⟦0⟧ (“tax collectors and prostitutes are going ahead of you into the kingdom”). Manuscripts are notoriously tangled here. Some reverse the order of the sons and correspondingly the answer, and a few even have the leaders give the **wrong** answer. Textual critics still argue over which is original.

cites.words: οἱ τελῶναι καὶ αἱ πόρναι προάγουσιν ὑμᾶς

note.text: An allegory in which nearly everyone recognizes the characters. The owner finally sends ⟦0⟧ (“one beloved son”), the words of the baptismal voice. Matthew draws the starkest conclusion: the kingdom ⟦1⟧ (“will be given to a people producing its fruits”). The quotation of Psalm 118, ⟦2⟧ (“the stone the builders rejected”), may rest on a Hebrew pun: *ben* (son), *eben* (stone).

cites.words: δοθήσεται ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺς καρποὺς αὐτῆς

lede.text: A vineyard owner sends servants and finally his son to collect his rent, and the tenants kill them all. It is the most openly allegorical of the Synoptic parables, and the Jerusalem leaders recognize at once that it is aimed at them. Small differences in the order of events show the evangelists reading Jesus' death into the story.

body.text: Mark's opening echoes Isaiah 5, the Song of the Vineyard, in which Israel is God's vineyard: ⟦0⟧ (“a man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the winepress, and built a tower”). Every listener would recognize the source. But in Jesus' version the vineyard isn't at fault, the **tenants** are. The target has moved from the people to their leaders, and Matthew says explicitly that ⟦1⟧ (“they knew he was speaking about them”).

cites.words: Ἀμπελῶνα ἄνθρωπος ἐφύτευσεν καὶ περιέθηκεν φραγμὸν καὶ ὤρυξεν ὑπολήνιον καὶ ᾠκοδόμησεν πύργον

sections.heading: Killed, then thrown out, or thrown out, then killed?

body.text:
Mark's order is ⟦0⟧ (“they killed him and threw him out of the vineyard”), leaving the body unburied, which was a final insult. Matthew and Luke both reverse it: ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ (“they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him”).

Why? Jesus was crucified **outside** the city walls (John 19:20; Hebrews 13:12 makes a point of it). Both later evangelists seem to have adjusted the parable to match the Passion. It is a minor agreement that both theories can explain as independent editing toward the same, obvious goal.

cites.words: ἀπέκτειναν αὐτόν καὶ ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος
ἐξέβαλον ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος καὶ ἀπέκτειναν
ἐκβαλόντες αὐτὸν ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος ἀπέκτειναν

body.text: Mark's owner has ⟦0⟧ (“one beloved son”), the same phrase as the heavenly voice at the baptism. Luke gives the owner an inner monologue, ⟦1⟧ (“what shall I do?”), and a hesitant hope: ⟦2⟧ (“**perhaps** they will respect him”). The tenants' logic, ⟦3⟧ (“this is the heir”), may reflect a real legal situation: property with no heir could be claimed by those in possession.

In Matthew the audience pronounces its own sentence: ⟦0⟧ (“he will put those wretches to a wretched death”), a Greek wordplay. Matthew then adds a verse found only in his Gospel: ⟦1⟧ (“the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a people producing its fruits”). The verse has a long history of supersessionist readings, in which the Church replaces Israel. Many scholars argue that in context it targets Jerusalem's leaders, not the Jewish people.

In Luke the audience recoils: ⟦2⟧ (“may it never be!”). All three close with Psalm 118:22, ⟦3⟧ (“the stone the builders rejected”). There is a pun in Hebrew, where *ben* (son) and *eben* (stone) sound alike.

cites.words: ἀρθήσεται ἀφ ὑμῶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ δοθήσεται ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺς καρποὺς αὐτῆς

note.text: The questioners open with flattery, ⟦0⟧ (literally “you don't look at people's faces”, that is, you show no partiality). Jesus asks to see a coin: ⟦1⟧ (“whose **image** is this, and inscription?”). A denarius of Tiberius proclaimed him son of the divine Augustus. Readers who knew Genesis 1:27, where humans bear God's *eikōn*, could hear the second half of the answer as a claim on the whole person.

cites.words: οὐ γὰρ βλέπεις εἰς πρόσωπον ἀνθρώπων
Τίνος ἡ εἰκὼν αὕτη καὶ ἡ ἐπιγραφή

note.text: The Sadducees, who denied resurrection (Josephus and Acts 23:8 agree), pose a riddle about one woman with seven husbands. Mark's Jesus answers bluntly, ⟦0⟧ (“you are badly mistaken”). Luke softens that and adds two lines of his own: the risen are ⟦1⟧ (“like angels”, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament) and ⟦2⟧ (“for all live to him”).

Jesus takes the offensive with a riddle from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted or alluded to in the New Testament: ⟦0⟧ (“the Lord said to my lord”). If David calls the Messiah “lord”, how can he be merely David's son? All three keep this short exchange close to Mark's wording; Matthew and Luke share long runs of identical words with him here.

Mark explains the widow's two coins with a Roman one: ⟦0⟧ (“two *lepta*, which make a *quadrans*”). Explaining Greek money in Roman terms is one of the clues that point to an audience in the Roman west, possibly Rome itself. Luke drops the explanation and uses the rare word ⟦1⟧ (“needy”). The punchline: she gave ⟦2⟧ (“her whole **life**”), that is, her whole livelihood.

The discourse begins with a prophecy: ⟦0⟧ (“not one stone will be left on another”). The Romans destroyed the temple in 70 CE. In Mark and Luke the disciples ask when and what sign. Matthew adds a second question about ⟦1⟧ (“your **coming**”). *Parousia*, the technical term for the second coming, appears in the Gospels only in this chapter of Matthew. Mark calls the wars and earthquakes ⟦2⟧ (“the beginning of **birth pains**”).

cites.words: οὐ μὴ ἀφεθῇ ὧδε λίθος ἐπὶ λίθον

note.text: Mark's ⟦0⟧ (“the gospel must **first** be preached to all nations”) becomes in Matthew a timetable: ⟦1⟧ (“and **then** the end will come”). Matthew had already used Mark's persecution sayings in his mission speech (10:17–22). Luke's version contains a tension he doesn't resolve: some will be killed, yet ⟦2⟧ (“not a hair of your head will perish”).

cites.words: εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη πρῶτον δεῖ κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον
θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὑμῶν οὐ μὴ ἀπόληται

note.text: Mark's ⟦0⟧ (“the abomination of desolation standing”) uses a **masculine** participle with a neuter noun, as if it were a person. Then he addresses his audience directly: ⟦1⟧ (“let the **reader** understand”), a sign that this is a written text. Luke replaces the cryptic phrase with plain history: ⟦2⟧ (“Jerusalem surrounded by armies”). Only Matthew adds a prayer that flight not come ⟦3⟧ (“on a sabbath”).

Matthew merges Mark's warning about false messiahs with Q sayings that Luke places in chapter 17, which accounts for the 57 minor agreements. Matthew's lightning illustrates the ⟦0⟧ (“coming of the Son of Man”). The images of who is “taken” differ: Matthew's ⟦1⟧ (“two in a field”), Luke's ⟦2⟧ (“two in one bed”). Next to the flood comparison, being taken may mean judgment, not rescue.

cites.words: ἡ παρουσία τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου

note.text: The climax quotes Daniel 7:13: ⟦0⟧ (“they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds”). Matthew adds ⟦1⟧ (“the **sign** of the Son of Man”), the nations' mourning from Zechariah 12, and ⟦2⟧ (“with a great trumpet”). Luke adds cosmic anxiety on earth among the nations, ⟦3⟧ (“perplexed at the roaring of the sea”).

cites.words: ὄψονται τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐρχόμενον ἐν νεφέλαις
τὸ σημεῖον τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου

note.text: Matthew and Mark agree in about 89% of their words here, one of the highest scores on the site. The passage holds two of the most debated verses in the Gospels: ⟦0⟧ (“this generation will not pass away”) until all this happens, and ⟦1⟧ (“not even the Son”) knows the day or hour. Luke keeps the first but omits the second entirely; some Matthew manuscripts drop “nor the Son” (see Variants).

cites.words: οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη

note.text: A two-verse summary found only in Luke: Jesus taught in the temple by day and spent the nights ⟦0⟧ (“on the mount called Olivet”), and all the people ⟦1⟧ (“came early in the morning”) to hear him. A group of medieval manuscripts (family 13) inserts the story of the woman caught in adultery **right here**, after Luke 21:38, a sign of how that story floated before it settled in John 8.

cites.words: εἰς τὸ ὄρος τὸ καλούμενον Ἐλαιῶν

note.text: Only Matthew tells this parable of bridesmaids waiting with lamps: ⟦0⟧ (“five were foolish and five wise”). *Mōrai* gives English “moron”; the same pair of words ended the Sermon on the Mount (the wise and foolish builders). Many scholars think the delay of the bridegroom reflects the early church's experience of the delayed return of Christ; read traditionally, Jesus is warning that his return may come later than expected. The moral: ⟦1⟧ (“so keep awake”).

cites.words: πέντε δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἦσαν μωραὶ καὶ πέντε φρόνιμοι

note.text: Only Matthew has this scene, the climax of Jesus' teaching in his Gospel. The Son of Man separates the nations ⟦0⟧ (“as a shepherd separates sheep from goats”). The criterion is care for ⟦1⟧ (“one of the least of these my brothers”). Whether that means anyone in need or specifically Jesus' disciples (as “little ones” and “brothers” often do in Matthew) is a long-running debate.

cites.words: ὥσπερ ὁ ποιμὴν ἀφορίζει τὰ πρόβατα ἀπὸ τῶν ἐρίφων
ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων

note.text: In Mark the priests simply promise Judas ⟦0⟧ (“money”), and Mark gives no motive. Matthew has Judas ask the price and names it: ⟦1⟧ (“thirty silver pieces”), the wage paid to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah 11:12. Luke supplies a supernatural motive instead: ⟦2⟧ (“Satan entered Judas”). John says the same, at the supper (13:27).

In the Synoptics the Last Supper is a Passover meal, ⟦0⟧ (“when they sacrificed the Passover lamb”). The disciples are to look for ⟦1⟧ (“a man carrying a water jar”), a recognizable sign since carrying water was usually women's work. Luke names the two disciples as ⟦2⟧ (“Peter and John”), the pair who lead the church together in Acts 3–4.

Mark's ⟦0⟧ (“one who is eating with me”) echoes Psalm 41:9. Only Matthew has Judas himself ask ⟦1⟧ (“surely not I, Rabbi?”) and receive the enigmatic ⟦2⟧ (“you have said it”). Only John introduces the disciple ⟦3⟧ (“whom Jesus loved”). His scene closes with four words: ⟦4⟧ (“and it was **night**”).

Two traditions of the words over the cup. Mark and Matthew: ⟦0⟧ (“my blood **of the covenant**”), echoing Exodus 24:8. Luke: ⟦1⟧ (“the **new** covenant in my blood”), almost exactly Paul's wording in 1 Corinthians 11:25. Matthew alone adds ⟦2⟧ (“for the forgiveness of sins”), a phrase he had removed from Mark's description of John's baptism.

cites.words: ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου

lede.text: Jesus' words over the bread and cup survive in four early versions: Mark, Matthew, Luke, and Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians (11:23–25), written about twenty years before Mark. Laid side by side, they fall into two families, and the differences show how a sacred formula was handed on and shaped in worship.

body.text:
Matthew follows Mark closely here; the alignment above shows about 70% of Matthew's words taken from Mark. Mark's bread-word is bare: ⟦0⟧ (“take, this is my body”). Matthew adds one verb, ⟦1⟧ (“eat”), and turns Mark's narration that “they all drank” into a command, ⟦2⟧ (“drink from it, all of you”). Both read like the words of a liturgy.

Luke belongs to the other family, the one Paul also quotes. His bread is ⟦3⟧ (“given **for you**”), followed by ⟦4⟧ (“do this in remembrance of me”). The command to remember appears only in Luke and Paul. His cup is ⟦5⟧ (“the new covenant in my blood”), recalling Jeremiah 31's promise of a new covenant, where Mark's ⟦6⟧ recalls Moses sprinkling “the blood of the covenant” at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).

cites.words: Λάβετε τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου
τοῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν
ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου

sections.heading: Luke's two cups, and a famous textual problem

body.text:
Only Luke has a cup **before** the bread: ⟦0⟧ (“take this and share it among yourselves”), and then a second cup ⟦1⟧ (“after supper”). A Passover meal involved several cups of wine, so the sequence may reflect the meal's real shape.

There is a complication. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts lack everything from “given for you” to the end of verse 20, which leaves Luke with a cup-then-bread order. In the nineteenth century Westcott and Hort counted the longer text as a later addition. The discovery of the early papyrus P75, which contains it, has persuaded most modern editors that it is original.

cites.words: Λάβετε τοῦτο καὶ διαμερίσατε εἰς ἑαυτούς

body.text: All three Synoptics keep a vow that points beyond the meal. Jesus will not drink again ⟦0⟧ (“of the fruit of the vine”) until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. Matthew adds two words that turn it into a promise of reunion: ⟦1⟧ (“**with you**”). Luke moves the vow before the bread, so that his supper begins with the end of the age in view: Jesus will not eat the Passover again ⟦2⟧ (“until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”).

cites.words: ἕως ὅτου πληρωθῇ ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ

body.text:
Matthew's cup is poured out ⟦0⟧ (“for the forgiveness of sins”). Mark had used that phrase for John the Baptist's baptism (1:4), and Matthew left it out there. He seems to have kept it for this moment, so that forgiveness is tied to Jesus' death rather than John's water.

John's Gospel tells the Last Supper across five chapters, yet it has no words over bread and cup at all. In their place is the foot-washing, and the eucharistic language appears instead in the Bread of Life discourse after the feeding of the five thousand (6:51–58). Whether John assumes his readers know the ritual, or deliberately moves its meaning elsewhere, is an open question.

note.text: Only Mark has the rooster crow **twice**: ⟦0⟧ (“before the rooster crows twice”). The other Gospels simplify to one crow. Luke's version is tender, and the Greek pronouns matter: Satan has demanded ⟦1⟧ (“you”, plural, all of you), but Jesus prayed ⟦2⟧ (“for **you**”, singular, Peter). John places the prediction after the ⟦3⟧ (“new commandment”).

A strange exchange found only in Luke. Jesus reverses his earlier mission instructions: ⟦0⟧ (“whoever has none should sell his cloak and buy a sword”), so that Isaiah 53:12 (“counted among the lawless”) is fulfilled. The disciples take him literally and produce two swords, and he replies ⟦1⟧, either “that is enough” or, more likely, an exasperated “enough of this!”

cites.words: ὁ μὴ ἔχων πωλησάτω τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀγορασάτω μάχαιραν

note.text: Mark's Jesus is overwhelmed, ⟦0⟧ (“began to be distressed and agitated”), and prays in Aramaic: ⟦1⟧. Matthew has him fall ⟦2⟧ (“on his face”). Luke's version is calmer, apart from the disputed verse about ⟦3⟧ (“his sweat like drops of blood”). John has no agony at all; only he calls the place ⟦4⟧ (“a garden”).

cites.words: ὁ ἱδρὼς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος

lede.text: No scene shows the Gospels' different portraits of Jesus more clearly than the night in Gethsemane. Mark's Jesus is overwhelmed, Matthew's prays the Lord's Prayer, and Luke's, in the oldest manuscripts, is composed. John leaves out the struggle altogether.

sections.heading: Mark: horror and the Aramaic word for Father

body.text:
Mark uses strong verbs: Jesus ⟦0⟧ (“began to be utterly dismayed and distressed”). He says ⟦1⟧ (“my soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death”), borrowing the refrain of Psalms 42–43. He does not kneel; he ⟦2⟧ (“kept falling to the ground”).

The prayer opens with ⟦3⟧, the Aramaic *abba* followed by its Greek equivalent. Paul uses exactly this pair as the prayer of believers (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6), which suggests that early Greek-speaking Christians remembered and repeated Jesus' own word.

cites.words: Περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου

sections.heading: Matthew: the Lord's Prayer under pressure

body.text: Matthew keeps Mark's structure of three returns to the sleeping disciples, but gives the second prayer its own words: ⟦0⟧ (“your will be done”). That is word for word the third petition of the Lord's Prayer as Matthew records it (6:10). Matthew's Jesus prays in his darkest hour the prayer he taught on the mountain, and the reader who knows the Sermon hears the echo.

sections.heading: Luke: kneeling, and two disputed verses

body.text:
Luke's account is shorter and calmer. Jesus withdraws ⟦0⟧ (“about a stone's throw”) and ⟦1⟧ (“knelt”), the posture of prayer in Acts. There is one prayer, not three: ⟦2⟧ (“yet not my will but yours be done”). Luke even excuses the disciples, who are sleeping ⟦3⟧ (“from grief”).

Then come the most debated verses in Luke's Passion: an angel strengthening Jesus (⟦4⟧) and ⟦5⟧ (“his sweat became **like** drops of blood”; a simile, not a medical claim). They are missing from P75 and Codex Vaticanus. Some scholars argue that they don't fit Luke's otherwise composed Jesus and were added; others, that orthodox scribes cut them because they made Jesus look too weak. The site's data marks them as doubtful text.

cites.words: πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω
ὁ ἱδρὼς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος

body.text: John has no agony in the garden. His Jesus addressed the temptation earlier, rhetorically: “shall I say, ‘Father, save me from this hour’? No, for this purpose I came” (12:27). At the arrest the Synoptic prayer about the cup is turned into its opposite: ⟦0⟧ (“the cup the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?”). The tradition is the same, but the Christology has changed: in John, Jesus is never a victim of his hour, only its master.

cites.words: τὸ ποτήριον ὃ δέδωκέν μοι ὁ πατὴρ οὐ μὴ πίω αὐτό

note.text: Each Gospel adds something. Mark: a young man flees ⟦0⟧ (“wearing only a linen cloth”), a mystery that has produced many theories. Matthew: ⟦1⟧ (“all who take the sword will perish by the sword”). Luke: Jesus ⟦2⟧ (“touched the ear and healed him”). John: the soldiers fall back at ⟦3⟧ (“I am”), and only John names Peter as the swordsman and the servant as Malchus.

cites.words: πάντες γὰρ οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀπολοῦνται

note.text: Mark's Jesus answers the high priest plainly: ⟦0⟧ (“I am”). Matthew's answer is evasive, ⟦1⟧ (“you have said so”), and so is Luke's. The famous minor agreement comes next. Mark's guards blindfold Jesus and say only “Prophesy!”. Matthew and Luke **both** add the same five words: ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ (“Who is it that struck you?”). In Matthew, where there is no blindfold, the taunt makes little sense.

lede.text: The Jewish hearing is reported in three very different shapes. Mark and Matthew describe a night trial with witnesses and a death verdict; Luke, a morning session that issues no verdict; John, an informal interrogation by a former high priest. Inside this unit is also one of the most debated minor agreements in the Synoptic problem.

body.text:
Mark's trial begins as a failure: the witnesses' testimony is inconsistent, ⟦0⟧ (“their testimonies did not agree”), and Deuteronomy 19:15 required two witnesses who agreed. The high priest then asks directly, with a reverent substitute for God's name: ⟦1⟧ (“are you the Christ, the Son of the **Blessed One**?”).

All through Mark, Jesus has silenced those who named him. Now, at the moment it will cost him his life, he answers without qualification: ⟦2⟧ (“I am”). He then combines Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1, the Son of Man seated at the right hand and coming with the clouds. The high priest tears his garments, and the verdict is ⟦3⟧ (“deserving death”).

cites.words: Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ εὐλογητοῦ

sections.heading: Matthew and Luke: a guarded answer

body.text:
Both later Gospels make the answer less direct. In Matthew the high priest puts Jesus under oath, ⟦0⟧ (“I adjure you by the living God”), and Jesus replies ⟦1⟧ (“you have said it”). Luke splits the question in two, and Jesus first refuses: ⟦2⟧ (“if I tell you, you will not believe”). Then ⟦3⟧ (“you say that I am”).

Both add a time marker Mark lacks: Matthew's ⟦4⟧ and Luke's ⟦5⟧, each meaning “from now on”. Luke also drops the coming on the clouds: ⟦6⟧ (“the Son of Man will be **seated**”). The exaltation begins now, and the return can wait, a pattern seen throughout Luke–Acts.

cites.words: Ἐξορκίζω σε κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος
Ἐὰν ὑμῖν εἴπω οὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε
ἔσται ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καθήμενος

body.text:
In Mark the guards cover Jesus' face, strike him, and say ⟦0⟧ (“Prophesy!”). Matthew and Luke both add the same five Greek words: ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ (“who is it that struck you?”). In Luke the taunt makes sense, because he keeps the blindfold. Matthew has dropped the blindfold, so his guards demand that Jesus identify someone he can plainly see.

For the Two-Source hypothesis, which holds that Matthew and Luke used Mark independently, this is a hard case. Its defenders suggest that early scribes copied the line into Matthew from Luke, though no surviving manuscript of Matthew lacks it, or that both drew on a common oral version of the mockery. For Farrer and Griesbach advocates it is simple: one evangelist read the other.

John has no session of the council and no verdict. Jesus is taken ⟦0⟧ (“to Annas first”), the former high priest and father-in-law of Caiaphas, who questions him about his teaching. Jesus answers ⟦1⟧ (“I have spoken openly to the world”). In John the decision was already made back in chapter 11, after Lazarus was raised, and the whole Gospel has been a trial, with witnesses called and testimony given. The night hearing is a formality.

note.text: Matthew explains why Peter is recognized: ⟦0⟧ (“your **accent** gives you away”), a Galilean speaking in Jerusalem. Only Luke records that at the rooster's crow ⟦1⟧ (“the Lord turned and looked at Peter”). John's third questioner is ⟦2⟧ (“a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off”).

cites.words: ἡ λαλιά σου δῆλόν σε ποιεῖ
στραφεὶς ὁ κύριος ἐνέβλεψεν τῷ Πέτρῳ
συγγενὴς ὢν οὗ ἀπέκοψεν Πέτρος τὸ ὠτίον

lede.text: Peter's denial is one of the few stories told in all four Gospels with the same skeleton: a courtyard, a fire, three challenges, a rooster. It is also embarrassing to the movement's leading apostle, which most historians count as a mark of authenticity. The details each evangelist adds show what each wanted the story to mean.

body.text:
Mark sets up a split screen. Peter follows ⟦0⟧ (“at a distance”) and sits with the guards ⟦1⟧ (“warming himself”) while Jesus is tried inside. Then Mark cuts back and forth. Inside, Jesus answers the high priest with “I am”. Outside, Peter's answers escalate. First comes a lawyerly dodge, ⟦2⟧ (“I neither know nor understand what you mean”); then ⟦3⟧ (“he began to curse and swear”). The verb *anathematizein* has no object. Some scholars suggest that Peter was cursing Jesus, the ultimate denial, and that Mark tactfully left the object out.

Mark alone has the rooster crow twice, and ends with a puzzling phrase: ⟦4⟧, perhaps “he broke down and wept”. The meaning of *epibalōn* here is genuinely uncertain.

cites.words: Οὔτε οἶδα οὔτε ἐπίσταμαι σὺ τί λέγεις

body.text: Matthew and Luke both replace Mark's obscure ending with the same five words: ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ (“going outside, he wept bitterly”). Two independent editors could each have clarified Mark, but finding the **identical** five-word solution is harder to explain. Two-Source scholars point out that a few Old Latin manuscripts lack Luke 22:62, and argue that a scribe borrowed it from Matthew. On the Farrer view, Luke simply took it from Matthew.

Luke tells the denials **before** the trial, so they are not interleaved with it, and he softens Peter's words: there are no curses. He adds lighting, as a novelist might: the servant girl sees Peter ⟦0⟧ (“facing the firelight”) and stares. And he adds the most quoted detail of all: ⟦1⟧ (“the Lord turned and looked at Peter”). In Luke, Jesus is close enough to see him, which makes the moment personal rather than merely tragic.

cites.words: στραφεὶς ὁ κύριος ἐνέβλεψεν τῷ Πέτρῳ

sections.heading: John: “I am not”, and a second charcoal fire

body.text: John shapes the story with contrast. In the garden Jesus has just said “I am” (*egō eimi*) three times; in the courtyard Peter answers twice ⟦0⟧ (“I am **not**”). John's fire is an ⟦1⟧ (“a charcoal fire”). The word appears only one other time in the New Testament: on the beach after the resurrection, where the risen Jesus has made ⟦2⟧ and asks Peter ⟦3⟧ (“a third time”), “do you love me?” Three denials beside one charcoal fire are answered by three affirmations beside another.

note.text: A brief transition with almost no shared wording outside Mark–Matthew. Mark: ⟦0⟧ (“at once, early”) the council binds Jesus and hands him over. John adds a detail that sets his chronology apart. The accusers would not enter the governor's residence ⟦1⟧ (“so as not to be defiled, but to eat the Passover”). In John, then, the Passover meal has not yet happened, unless, as some harmonizers argue, “eat the Passover” means the festival's other sacrificial meals.

cites.words: ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν ἀλλὰ φάγωσιν τὸ πάσχα

note.text: Only Matthew tells this: Judas ⟦0⟧ (“seized with remorse”) returns the money and ⟦1⟧ (“hanged himself”). Acts 1:18, by Luke, gives a different account: Judas buys a field himself and falls headlong. Harmonizers since Augustine have combined them: he hanged himself, the body later fell, and the priests bought the field with his money, in his name. Matthew attributes his scripture to ⟦2⟧ (“Jeremiah the prophet”), though the words come mainly from Zechariah 11:12–13, blended with Jeremiah's potter and field purchase.

Pilate's question is word for word the same in all four Gospels: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Mark's Jesus replies ⟦0⟧ (“you say so”). Luke frames the trial with three explicitly political charges (⟦1⟧, “forbidding tribute to Caesar”) and three verdicts of innocence, the first ⟦2⟧ (“I find no guilt”). John turns it into a dialogue, ending in ⟦3⟧ (“what is truth?”).

lede.text: Pilate's first question is identical, word for word, in all four Gospels: ⟦0⟧ (“are you the King of the Jews?”). That is very rare across the Synoptics and John, and it suggests a fixed early memory. The charge on which Rome executed Jesus was a political one. From that shared starting point, each Gospel builds a very different trial.

cites.words: Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων

sections.heading: The shared core: two words and a silence

body.text: All three Synoptics give the same two-word reply: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧ (“you say so”). It is neither yes nor no. Then, in Mark and Matthew, Jesus says nothing more, ⟦2⟧ (“so that Pilate was amazed”). Early Christians heard Isaiah 53:7 in the silence: “like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.”

sections.heading: Luke: a political trial and three acquittals

body.text:
