Luke gives the accusers a precise indictment with three counts: ⟦0⟧ (“subverting our nation”), forbidding taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be a king. Readers know the second count is false, because Jesus had said “give to Caesar what is Caesar's” (20:25).

Luke then has Pilate declare Jesus innocent three times, ending with ⟦1⟧ (“a third time he said”): “I have found in him no cause for death.” The pattern matches Acts, where Roman officials repeatedly find Paul innocent. Many scholars see an apologetic aim: to show Roman readers that the movement's founder was no rebel, whatever the cross implied.

John stages the trial as a drama on two levels. Pilate goes back and forth between the accusers outside, who will not enter, and Jesus inside: ⟦0⟧ (“so Pilate went back into the praetorium”). Many commentators count seven alternating scenes. Inside, Jesus explains his kingship: ⟦1⟧. The preposition *ek* means “**from** this world”, its source, not that it is absent from this world.

John expands the Synoptic reply into a statement: ⟦2⟧ (“you say that I am a king”), “for this I was born, to testify to the truth.” Pilate's reply, ⟦3⟧ (“what is truth?”), gets no answer, and John's irony is that the person standing in front of him has already claimed to be the truth (14:6). By the end of the scene, the reader suspects that the judge is the one on trial.

cites.words: Εἰσῆλθεν οὖν πάλιν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον
Ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου

note.text: Only Luke has Pilate send Jesus to Herod Antipas, who is in Jerusalem for the festival. Herod ⟦0⟧ (“was very glad”), because he had long wanted to see a sign, a wish Luke planted at 9:9. Jesus says nothing. The scene ends with a bitter aside: ⟦1⟧ (“Herod and Pilate became friends that day”). In Acts 4:27 the church reads Psalm 2 as fulfilled by this alliance.

cites.words: ἐγένοντο δὲ φίλοι ὅ τε Ἡρῴδης καὶ ὁ Πιλᾶτος

note.text: In Matthew Pilate offers a choice between two men named Jesus: ⟦0⟧ (“Jesus Barabbas or Jesus called Christ”). Barabbas means “son of the father” in Aramaic. Most manuscripts lack the first “Jesus”, but modern editions print it. Only Matthew has Pilate's wife's dream and the hand-washing, followed by ⟦1⟧ (“his blood be on us and our children”), a line later used catastrophically to justify persecuting Jews.

cites.words: Ἰησοῦν τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἢ Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον χριστόν
Τὸ αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐφ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν

lede.text: Every Gospel includes the Barabbas episode, and none of them agrees with the others about who was to blame. Read in sequence, they show a steady shift: Pilate is made more reluctant and the Jewish crowd more responsible. That shift had grave consequences in later history.

body.text: Mark describes a custom: ⟦0⟧ (“at the festival he used to release one prisoner for them”). No source outside the Gospels mentions such a Passover amnesty, and historians debate it. Defenders note how sparse the sources are, and that the Mishnah (Pesachim 8:6) allows a Passover lamb to be slaughtered for someone promised release from prison. Barabbas is no ordinary prisoner. Mark places him ⟦1⟧ (“imprisoned with the insurrectionists”), Luke says he was jailed ⟦2⟧ (“for insurrection and murder”), and John calls him a ⟦3⟧, a word Josephus uses for armed rebels. The irony is sharp: Jesus is crucified as a would-be king, and a real insurrectionist goes free.

cites.words: Κατὰ δὲ ἑορτὴν ἀπέλυεν αὐτοῖς ἕνα δέσμιον

body.text: In Matthew, Pilate asks ⟦0⟧ (“Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus called Christ?”). Most manuscripts lack the first “Jesus”, but the third-century scholar Origen knew copies that had it, and disliked the idea of a sinner bearing the holy name. That is exactly why scribes might have removed it, and most modern editions now print it. In Aramaic *Bar-abba* means “son of the father”, so the crowd chooses between two sons of the father.

cites.words: Ἰησοῦν τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἢ Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον χριστόν

body.text:
**Mark**: Pilate knows the priests acted ⟦0⟧ (“out of envy”), but releases Barabbas ⟦1⟧ (“wishing to satisfy the crowd”). The phrase translates the Latin *satis facere*.

**Matthew**: Pilate's wife warns him after a dream; Pilate washes his hands, ⟦2⟧ (“I am innocent of this blood”), and ⟦3⟧ (“all the people”) take the blood on themselves and their children.

**Luke**: Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times and finally hands him over ⟦4⟧ (“to their will”).

**John**: the chief priests declare ⟦5⟧ (“we have no king but Caesar”), which in John's terms amounts to renouncing God's kingship.

cites.words: βουλόμενος τῷ ὄχλῳ τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι
Οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα εἰ μὴ Καίσαρα

body.text:
Outside the Gospels, Philo and Josephus portray Pilate as stubborn and brutal, not as a vacillating man pushed around by a crowd. Many historians therefore read the Gospels' increasingly sympathetic Pilate as reflecting the needs of Christians who lived under Rome and were in conflict with synagogues. Others reply that a governor facing a festival crowd, and wary of complaints reaching Rome, could well have hesitated as the Gospels describe.

Matthew 27:25 was later used to brand Jews collectively as “Christ-killers”, a charge that fueled centuries of persecution. The Catholic Church formally rejected it at the Second Vatican Council (*Nostra Aetate*, 1965), and most churches and New Testament scholars today read the verse within Matthew's own setting, a bitter dispute inside the Jewish community of the first century.

note.text: Mark's soldiers dress Jesus in ⟦0⟧ (“purple”), the imperial color, and Matthew in a soldier's scarlet cloak. They parody the salute to the emperor (*Ave Caesar*) with ⟦1⟧ (“Hail, King of the Jews!”). Luke omits this scene but has Herod's soldiers mock Jesus earlier (23:11). John moves the mockery into the middle of the trial.

Mark identifies Simon of Cyrene as ⟦0⟧ (“the father of Alexander and Rufus”), apparently men his readers knew. The soldiers ⟦1⟧ (“press into service”) him, a Persian loanword for compulsory service also used in Matthew 5:41. Only Luke has Jesus address the mourning women: ⟦2⟧ (“daughters of Jerusalem, don't weep for me”). In John, Jesus carries the cross himself.

cites.words: Θυγατέρες Ἰερουσαλήμ μὴ κλαίετε ἐπ ἐμέ

note.text: Mark gives a time: ⟦0⟧ (“it was the third hour”, about 9 a.m.). John has Pilate's trial still going at about the sixth hour (noon). Some harmonizers think John counts hours from midnight, the Roman civil way, making his “sixth hour” about 6 a.m. The charge differs slightly in each Gospel. John says it was written ⟦1⟧ (“in Hebrew, Latin and Greek”). Only Luke has the penitent criminal and the promise ⟦2⟧ (“today you will be with me in Paradise”).

cites.words: σήμερον μετ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ

lede.text: The Gospels describe the act of crucifixion in a single verb, ⟦0⟧ (“and they crucify him”), told in Mark's vivid present tense. Their attention goes elsewhere: to scripture, especially Psalm 22, to the mockers, to the placard over his head, and to the people who stood nearby.

body.text:
The details Mark chooses follow Psalm 22 closely. The soldiers ⟦0⟧ (“divide his garments, casting lots”), from Psalm 22:18. The passers-by mock him ⟦1⟧ (“shaking their heads”), from Psalm 22:7. Mark never says “this fulfilled the scripture”; he lets the allusions speak for themselves.

John quotes the psalm outright, ⟦2⟧ (“they divided my garments among them”), and then does something like what Matthew did with the donkeys. He takes the psalm's two parallel lines as two separate events: the garments are divided into four shares, and the seamless tunic is assigned by lot ⟦3⟧ (“the tunic”).

cites.words: διαμερίζονται τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ βάλλοντες κλῆρον

body.text:
In Mark everyone mocks him: passers-by, chief priests and scribes, and both men crucified with him. The priests' taunt is truer than they know: ⟦0⟧ (“he saved others; he cannot save himself”). In Mark's theology, that is precisely the point.

Luke separates the people from their leaders. ⟦1⟧ (“the people stood **watching**”); only the rulers sneer. Only one criminal mocks, ⟦2⟧ (“save yourself and us”), while the other asks to be remembered and receives the promise of Paradise.

cites.words: Ἄλλους ἔσωσεν ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται σῶσαι

body.text: The charge is worded differently in each Gospel. Mark's is shortest: ⟦0⟧ (“The King of the Jews”). John's is longest, ⟦1⟧ (“Jesus the Nazorean, the King of the Jews”); in Latin it gave Christian art the initials INRI. John alone says it was written in three languages and that Pilate refused to change it: ⟦2⟧ (“what I have written, I have written”). Pilate becomes an unwitting herald of the kingship he has just condemned.

cites.words: Ἰησοῦς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων

body.text: In the Synoptics the women watch ⟦0⟧ (“from a distance”). John places a small group ⟦1⟧ (“beside the cross”): Jesus' mother, her sister, Mary of Clopas, Mary Magdalene, and the Beloved Disciple. To them Jesus says ⟦2⟧ (“Woman, here is your son”). Neither Jesus' mother nor the Beloved Disciple appears at the cross in any other Gospel. Interpreters have read the scene as a founding of the new family of believers, which is a theme throughout John.

note.text: Each Gospel gives Jesus different last words. Mark and Matthew: Psalm 22:1, ⟦0⟧, in Aramaic, though Matthew's ⟦1⟧ is Hebrew, which makes the bystanders' confusion with “Elijah” more natural. Luke has Psalm 31:5, ⟦2⟧ (“into your hands I commit my spirit”). John: ⟦3⟧ (“it is finished”). Mark's centurion says “Son of God”; Luke's says ⟦4⟧ (“innocent/righteous”). Christian devotion has long combined them into the “seven last words”, treating each Gospel as preserving different sayings from the cross.

cites.words: Πάτερ εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου

lede.text: Each Gospel gives Jesus different last words. Mark and Matthew have a cry of abandonment, Luke a prayer of trust, John a declaration of completion. No passage shows more clearly that the evangelists were interpreters, not just recorders.

body.text:
Mark preserves the cry in Aramaic and then translates it: ⟦0⟧ (“Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani”), ⟦1⟧ (“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”). It is the opening line of Psalm 22, whose details Mark has been tracing throughout the crucifixion. Readers have argued for centuries over whether the cry is pure desolation or whether quoting the first line evokes the whole psalm, which ends in vindication. Mark does not say.

Matthew keeps the cry but gives the Hebrew form ⟦2⟧, which makes the bystanders' mishearing as a call to Elijah (*Ēlias*) easier to understand. A detail like this suggests Matthew knew the languages involved.

cites.words: Ὁ θεός μου ὁ θεός μου εἰς τί ἐγκατέλιπές με

body.text:
Luke leaves out the cry of abandonment entirely. In its place Jesus prays Psalm 31:5: ⟦0⟧ (“Father, into your hands I commit my spirit”). This was a traditional Jewish evening prayer, and Luke adds the address “Father”, so that Jesus' first recorded words in the Gospel (2:49, “my Father's house”) and his last both speak of the Father.

Luke's centurion also says something different. Mark's says ⟦1⟧ (“truly this man was God's Son”), the first human being in Mark to say so with understanding. Luke's says ⟦2⟧ (“surely this man was **innocent**” or “righteous”). Luke's interest, here as at Pilate's trial, is in Jesus' innocence.

cites.words: Πάτερ εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου
Ἀληθῶς οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος υἱὸς θεοῦ ἦν
Ὄντως ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος δίκαιος ἦν

body.text: John's Jesus remains in control to the end. He speaks ⟦0⟧ (“knowing that all was now completed”), and his final word is the same verb: ⟦1⟧ (“it is finished”, or “accomplished”). John doesn't say he “breathed his last”, as the Synoptics do (⟦2⟧); he says ⟦3⟧ (“he handed over the spirit”). The death is presented as an act Jesus performs, not something that happens to him.

cites.words: εἰδὼς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤδη πάντα τετέλεσται

sections.heading: Signs: the veil, the earthquake, the open tombs

body.text:
In Mark the moment of death is followed by one sign: ⟦0⟧ (“the curtain of the temple was torn in two”). The verb *schizō* appeared once before in Mark, when the heavens were ⟦1⟧ (“torn open”) at the baptism. The two tearings frame the Gospel.

Matthew adds an earthquake and something no other Gospel reports: ⟦2⟧ (“many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised”). Even many conservative commentators read this as apocalyptic imagery from Ezekiel 37 rather than as a report of events. Others take Matthew at his word: a real, if mysterious, event, a first sign of the general resurrection. Luke moves the veil earlier, to just before Jesus dies (⟦3⟧), and John omits it. In John, the sign is from Jesus' own body: ⟦4⟧ (“at once blood and water came out”).

cites.words: τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ ἐσχίσθη εἰς δύο
πολλὰ σώματα τῶν κεκοιμημένων ἁγίων ἠγέρθησαν
ἐσχίσθη δὲ τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ μέσον

note.text: Mark's Joseph of Arimathea is ⟦0⟧ (“a respected council member”) who ⟦1⟧ (“took courage”) to ask for the body. Luke's tomb is one ⟦2⟧ (“where no one had yet been laid”), echoing the colt no one had yet ridden. In John, Nicodemus brings ⟦3⟧ (“about a hundred pounds”) of myrrh and aloes, roughly 33 kg, a quantity fit for a king.

cites.words: οὗ οὐκ ἦν οὐδεὶς οὔπω κείμενος

note.text: Only Matthew has the chief priests ask Pilate to secure the tomb, ⟦0⟧ (“lest his disciples come and steal him”). Pilate replies ⟦1⟧, “you have a guard”, using a Latin loanword (*custodia*). The episode answers a rumor, still circulating when Matthew wrote, that the body had been stolen (see 28:15).

cites.words: μήποτε ἐλθόντες οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ κλέψωσιν αὐτὸν

note.text: Mark's Gospel, in its earliest manuscripts, ends here, with the women fleeing and telling no one: ⟦0⟧ (“for they were afraid”). Ending a sentence with *gar* is unusual, ending a book with it even more so. A minority of scholars, and many traditional readers, defend the longer ending (16:9–20) as original or apostolic, citing its presence in the great majority of manuscripts. Matthew adds an earthquake and an angel who ⟦1⟧ (“rolled away the stone”). Luke has ⟦2⟧ (“two men”; harmonizers note that Mark's one young man does not exclude a second), and the apostles dismiss the women's report as ⟦3⟧ (“nonsense”). John adds a footrace between Peter and the Beloved Disciple.

lede.text: All four Gospels agree that women went to Jesus' tomb on the first day of the week and found it empty. They disagree about almost everything else: how many women, how many angels, who saw what, and what the women did next. The disagreements are among the most studied in New Testament scholarship. Traditional harmonies, from Augustine on, fit the accounts together (one angel speaking does not exclude a second), and many readers see the untidy variety as a mark of independent witnesses rather than invention.

body.text:
In Mark a ⟦0⟧ (“young man”) in white tells the women ⟦1⟧ (“he has been raised; he is not here”) and sends them to tell ⟦2⟧ (“his disciples, **and Peter**”), naming the disciple who denied him. Then comes the most startling sentence in the Gospels: the women flee and say nothing to anyone, ⟦3⟧ (“for they were afraid”).

In the oldest manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, Mark ends there, on the Greek conjunction *gar*. Later scribes added at least two different endings to fill the gap, and the site marks those verses as disputed text. Whether Mark meant to end this way, or lost his last page, is still debated. Many scholars now think the abrupt ending is deliberate, leaving readers to finish the story themselves. A minority, along with many traditional readers, defend the longer ending as part of the Gospel.

cites.words: τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ τῷ Πέτρῳ

body.text: Matthew turns the scene into an apocalyptic event: ⟦0⟧ (“there was a great earthquake”), and an angel ⟦1⟧ (“rolled back the stone and sat on it”). Matthew also reverses Mark's ending. The women leave ⟦2⟧ (“with fear and great joy”) and run to tell the disciples. The fear stays, but joy is added and silence becomes proclamation.

cites.words: ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον καὶ ἐκάθητο ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ

sections.heading: Luke: two men, and a question

body.text: Luke has ⟦0⟧ (“two men”) in dazzling clothes. They ask ⟦1⟧ (“why do you look for the living among the dead?”) and tell the women to remember Jesus' words ⟦2⟧ (“in Galilee”). Mark had said the disciples would see Jesus *in* Galilee; Luke's resurrection appearances all happen around Jerusalem, so Galilee becomes a place remembered, not a destination. When the women report, the apostles think it ⟦3⟧ (“nonsense”). It is a striking admission for a Gospel to make about its own heroes.

cites.words: Τί ζητεῖτε τὸν ζῶντα μετὰ τῶν νεκρῶν

body.text:
Luke 24:12 and John 20 share an unusual cluster of wording. In both, a disciple runs to the tomb and ⟦0⟧ / ⟦1⟧ (“stooping down, he sees the linen cloths”). In John the Beloved Disciple ⟦2⟧ (“outran Peter”) and, once inside, ⟦3⟧ (“saw and believed”).

Luke 24:12 is missing from Codex Bezae, so Westcott and Hort treated it as a later harmonization with John. The verse is in P75, and most modern editions accept it. If it is original, it is among the strongest evidence that Luke and John drew on a shared tradition, or that one knew the other.

note.text: Matthew's women meet Jesus on the road and ⟦0⟧ (“took hold of his feet”). John's Mary Magdalene recognizes him only when he says her name, and answers ⟦1⟧. He then says ⟦2⟧, a present imperative better rendered “stop clinging to me” than the traditional “touch me not”. The longer ending of Mark describes Mary as the woman ⟦3⟧ (“from whom he had cast out seven demons”), a detail drawn from Luke 8:2.

lede.text: The first person to see the risen Jesus, according to Matthew, John and the added ending of Mark, was a woman, or a group of women. That fact is all the more striking because women's testimony counted for little in the ancient world, and Paul's list of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5–8) does not mention them at all.

body.text: Matthew's appearance is brief and physical. Jesus meets the women with an ordinary greeting, ⟦0⟧ (“Greetings!”), and they ⟦1⟧ (“took hold of his feet and worshipped him”). Holding his feet answers any suggestion that they saw a ghost. Jesus then repeats the angel's message almost word for word, with one change: the disciples are now ⟦2⟧ (“my **brothers**”). The ones who fled are not disowned.

cites.words: ἐκράτησαν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας καὶ προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ

body.text:
John tells one of the most carefully crafted recognition scenes in ancient literature. Mary Magdalene, weeping, is asked ⟦0⟧ (“whom are you looking for?”), the same question Jesus asked the first disciples (1:38) and the arresting soldiers (18:4). She mistakes him for ⟦1⟧ (“the gardener”). Then he says one word, her name, ⟦2⟧, and she knows him, as Jesus had said the sheep know the shepherd's voice when he “calls his own sheep by name” (10:3).

His next words are puzzling: ⟦3⟧ (“do not cling to me”, or “stop holding on to me”). The present tense suggests stopping an action already under way, so this is no ban on touch. Thomas will be invited to touch the wounds a week later. Jesus' presence is about to take a new form, ⟦4⟧ (“I am ascending to my Father and your Father”).

cites.words: Ἀναβαίνω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου καὶ πατέρα ὑμῶν

body.text: The added ending of Mark (16:9–20) summarizes appearances that look like a digest of the other Gospels. It begins ⟦0⟧ (“he appeared first to Mary Magdalene”), then mentions two travellers in the country (much like Luke's Emmaus story) and a commissioning of the eleven. Most scholars date it to the early second century. Its wording is uncharacteristic of Mark, and it is absent from the earliest manuscripts. Its defenders point out that it stands in the great majority of manuscripts and that Irenaeus quoted it around 180 CE. The site's data marks it as a later addition, but it is a valuable early witness to how Christians combined the four Gospels.

note.text: Only Matthew tells this. The guards are bribed to say ⟦0⟧ (“his disciples came by night and stole him while we slept”). Matthew adds a rare aside to his readers: the story ⟦1⟧ (“has been spread among Jews to this day”). In the next century, Justin Martyr also reports this counter-claim.

cites.words: Οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ νυκτὸς ἐλθόντες ἔκλεψαν αὐτὸν ἡμῶν κοιμωμένων
διεφημίσθη ὁ λόγος οὗτος παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις μέχρι τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας

note.text: Only Luke tells this story in full. The two disciples' ⟦0⟧ (“eyes were held”) until a meal, where Jesus repeats the four actions of the feeding and the Last Supper: ⟦1⟧ (“took the bread, blessed, broke, gave”). Mark's longer ending condenses it into one sentence, ⟦2⟧ (“he appeared in another form”), evidence that its author knew Luke.

cites.words: λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον εὐλόγησεν καὶ κλάσας ἐπεδίδου

note.text: Four very different scenes. Matthew's is on a mountain, and admits that ⟦0⟧ (“some doubted”); it ends with ⟦1⟧ (“I am with you”), which echoes “Emmanuel, God with us” (1:23). Luke insists on physical reality: ⟦2⟧ (“flesh and bones”) and a piece of broiled fish. In John, Jesus ⟦3⟧ (“breathed on”) them, the verb of Genesis 2:7 in the Septuagint. Mark's longer ending promises they will ⟦4⟧ (“pick up snakes”).

lede.text: Each Gospel ends with Jesus commissioning his followers, and each ending sums up its Gospel. Matthew's is on a mountain in Galilee, Luke's in a room in Jerusalem, John's behind locked doors. Placed together, they show four theologies of mission, and very little shared wording.

sections.heading: Matthew: the mountain and the Great Commission

body.text:
On a Galilean mountain, which recalls the Sermon on the Mount and Moses on Sinai, the eleven worship, ⟦0⟧ (“but some doubted”). The Greek can mean that some of them doubted, or that all did. Matthew includes the doubt, even at the end.

The commission is ⟦1⟧ (“make disciples of all nations”), reversing the earlier instruction to go only to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6). The triple baptismal formula ⟦2⟧ is unique in the Gospels and probably reflects the practice of Matthew's church; traditional readers take it as Jesus' own command, which the church then followed. The final promise, ⟦3⟧ (“I am with you”), echoes Emmanuel, “God with us”, from the first chapter (1:23).

cites.words: εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος

body.text:
Luke's Jesus insists on his physical body: ⟦0⟧ (“touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones”). Then he eats ⟦1⟧ (“a piece of broiled fish”). Luke seems to be answering people who said the disciples had seen only a ghost.

The commission is framed the way Acts will tell the story: ⟦2⟧ (“repentance and forgiveness of sins to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem”). Luke's second volume begins exactly where this verse points.

cites.words: ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει
μετάνοιαν καὶ ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ Ἰερουσαλήμ

body.text:
In John the risen Jesus comes through locked doors and says ⟦0⟧ (“peace be with you”). Then ⟦1⟧ (“he breathed on them”). The same rare verb appears in the Greek Old Testament when God breathes life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and into the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). John's Pentecost happens on Easter evening, as a new creation.

The saying about forgiving sins, ⟦2⟧ (“if you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven”), parallels Matthew's “binding and loosing” (16:19, 18:18) but uses different words. That points to a shared tradition reached by separate paths, not to copying.

cites.words: ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀφέωνται αὐτοῖς

body.text: The longer ending of Mark has its own version: ⟦0⟧ (“preach the gospel to all creation”), followed by promises of signs including handling snakes and drinking poison. The wording is closer to a blend of Matthew and Luke than to anything in Mark, which is one of several reasons scholars consider these verses a later addition.

cites.words: κηρύξατε τὸ εὐαγγέλιον πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει

note.text: Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus blessing the disciples and parting from them, and some manuscripts add ⟦0⟧ (“and he was carried up into heaven”). Luke's Gospel seems to place this on Easter day itself; his second volume, Acts, places it forty days later. Since the same author wrote both, many readers take the Gospel's ending as a compressed summary. The longer ending of Mark adds that he ⟦1⟧ (“sat at the right hand of God”), the language of Psalm 110.

teaser.text: Matthew and Luke give John the Baptist's tirade in Greek that is nearly identical, word for word, in a passage Mark doesn't have.

body.text: Start with ⟦0⟧ (*gennēmata echidnōn*, "brood of vipers") and keep reading. For more than sixty words Matthew and Luke agree in vocabulary, grammar and word order, with a run of 24 identical words. Even the tiny differences look like editing: Matthew's singular ⟦1⟧ ("fruit worthy") against Luke's plural ⟦2⟧ ("fruits worthy"), and "do not presume to say" against Luke's ⟦3⟧ ("do not begin to say"). Oral retelling rarely produces agreement this exact. It points to a shared *written* Greek source. Because Mark lacks the passage, the classic explanation is a lost collection of sayings that scholars call **Q** (from German *Quelle*, "source"). The main alternative, the Farrer hypothesis, says Luke simply copied Matthew. The early church's own view, that Matthew wrote first, would also explain the agreement without Q.

teaser.text: The Greek edition used here has Mark's Jesus "becoming angry" before he heals a leper. Matthew and Luke have no emotion at all.

body.text: Most English Bibles read "moved with compassion" in Mark 1:41. But one important early Greek manuscript (Codex Bezae) and several Old Latin translations read ⟦0⟧ (*orgistheis*, "becoming angry"), and the SBL Greek New Testament prints it. Textual critics often prefer the harder reading, on the logic that a scribe is more likely to soften an angry Jesus than to invent one. Two verses later Mark adds that Jesus ⟦1⟧ ("sternly warning him (literally, snorting at him), immediately drove him out"). Now compare the parallels: Matthew and Luke reproduce the healing almost word for word (⟦2⟧) but drop *both* emotional verbs. Whatever Mark originally wrote, his Jesus has a rough edge that the later Gospels sand off. Readers of English rarely see it.

teaser.text: At Jesus' trial, Matthew and Luke independently add the same five Greek words to Mark. Or did they?

body.text: In Mark the guards blindfold Jesus, beat him and say just ⟦0⟧ ("Prophesy!"). Matthew and Luke both complete the taunt with the same five words: ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ (*tis estin ho paisas se*, "Who is it that struck you?"). If, as most scholars think, Matthew and Luke each used Mark *without knowing each other*, how did they make the identical addition? This is the most famous of the **minor agreements**, places where Matthew and Luke agree against Mark. Defenders of the Two-Source theory suggest a coincidence, oral tradition, or an early scribe harmonizing the texts. Supporters of the Farrer theory see it as evidence that Luke had read Matthew. Our alignment finds hundreds of smaller agreements like it, and you can browse them passage by passage.

teaser.text: In our oldest manuscripts, Mark stops with frightened women and the word "for". Everything after was added later.

body.text: The two oldest complete Bibles, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century), end Mark at 16:8: ⟦0⟧ ("they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid"). Ending a sentence, let alone a book, on γάρ (*gar*, "for") is startling in Greek. Later scribes supplied endings. A one-sentence "shorter ending" (⟦1⟧) and the familiar "longer ending" (16:9–20) both appear in this edition inside double brackets, the editors' sign that they are not original. In this site those words carry a dashed outline. Notice that the longer ending reads like a digest of the other Gospels: an appearance to Mary Magdalene (⟦2⟧), two travelers in the country, a commission to preach. Matthew and Luke, following Mark, each write their own resurrection appearances, as if they too received a Mark that stopped at 16:8. A minority of scholars still defend the longer ending, which appears in the great majority of later manuscripts and was known to Irenaeus in the 2nd century.

teaser.text: The other three put the overturning of the tables in Jesus' final week. John puts it in chapter 2.

body.text: On the map, follow the gold ribbon that runs from the *end* of the Synoptic Gospels to the *beginning* of John. In Matthew, Mark and Luke, the temple incident triggers the plot to kill Jesus. John places it at the start of the ministry and gives it a different trigger for the arrest (the raising of Lazarus). The wording differs too. Only John has the whip, ⟦0⟧ ("a whip of cords"), the cattle and sheep, and the words ⟦1⟧ ("stop making my Father's house a house of trade"). The Synoptics share a scriptural quotation instead ("a house of prayer… a den of robbers"). Scholars debate whether there were two incidents, whether John moved it for theological reasons, or whether John preserves the earlier chronology. The data shows how little wording John shares with the others here.

cites.words: μὴ ποιεῖτε τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου οἶκον ἐμπορίου

teaser.text: Luke's version is noticeably shorter than Matthew's, and the familiar ending is in neither Gospel's oldest manuscripts.

body.text: Matthew opens ⟦0⟧ ("Our Father in the heavens"). Luke has just ⟦1⟧ (*Pater*, "Father"). Luke also lacks "your will be done" and "deliver us from the evil one". Yet where the two overlap, the Greek is strikingly close. Both use the rare word ἐπιούσιον (*epiousion*), traditionally "daily", a word almost unknown elsewhere in Greek, whose meaning is still debated. Many scholars think Luke's shorter form is closer to the original and that Matthew's reflects liturgical use. Luke, however, sets the prayer on a different occasion, and many traditional readers think Jesus taught it more than once, in two forms. And the doxology Protestants know ("for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory") is absent from both in the modern critical text. Switch the variant layer to the King James Greek in Matthew 6:13 to watch it appear.

cites.words: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς

teaser.text: In Mark, Jesus seems to deny that he is good. Matthew rewrites the question.

body.text: In Mark a man runs up and calls Jesus "good teacher". Jesus replies ⟦0⟧ ("Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone"). Luke keeps this almost exactly. Matthew changes it to ⟦1⟧ ("Why do you ask me about the good?"), and in his version the man calls Jesus "teacher" and asks what good *deed* he must do. The rest of the passage tracks Mark closely, which makes the change stand out. Under Markan priority, Matthew is smoothing a line that could be read as Jesus disclaiming goodness. Under the Griesbach hypothesis, Mark would have to be roughening Matthew, which most scholars find less likely. Small edits like this one are a main reason Markan priority is the majority view.

cites.words: Τί με ἐρωτᾷς περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ

teaser.text: Jesus' final words differ in every Gospel, and so does the verb for his death.

body.text: Mark and Matthew give only a cry of abandonment, kept in Aramaic (Matthew gives a more Hebrew form): ⟦0⟧ ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", from Psalm 22). Luke does not include it. His Jesus dies quoting Psalm 31 in trust: ⟦1⟧ ("Father, into your hands I commit my spirit"). John has a single word, ⟦2⟧ (*tetelestai*, "It is finished" or "It has been accomplished"). Even the death is narrated differently: Mark's ⟦3⟧ ("he breathed out"), Matthew's ⟦4⟧ ("he let go of his spirit"), John's ⟦5⟧ ("he handed over his spirit"). Each wording fits its Gospel's portrait: anguish, trust, completion. Christian tradition has long read them together, as different sayings spoken from the cross, the “seven last words”.

cites.words: Πάτερ εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου

teaser.text: "Let him who is without sin cast the first stone" is missing from John's earliest manuscripts.

body.text: John 7:53–8:11 is one of the best-loved stories in the Gospels, and almost certainly not part of the original John. It is absent from the earliest papyri and from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. In later manuscripts it appears in different places: after John 7:52, at the end of John, and in some cases after *Luke* 21:38. Its vocabulary is unlike John's elsewhere, and some scholars note it reads more like Luke. Modern editions print it in double brackets, which is why every word here, from ⟦0⟧ ("he was writing with his finger on the ground") to ⟦1⟧ ("the one of you without sin"), carries a dashed outline. Many scholars nonetheless think it preserves a genuinely early tradition about Jesus that circulated before it found a home in John.

cites.words: τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν

teaser.text: Mark says Jesus *could not* do miracles in his hometown. Matthew's version is more careful.

body.text: Mark says it bluntly: ⟦0⟧ ("he was not able to do any mighty work there"), except for healing a few sick people. Matthew turns inability into choice: ⟦1⟧ ("he did not do many mighty works there"), and he attaches the cause directly: "because of their unbelief". Another edit sits a few verses earlier. Mark's townsfolk ask ⟦2⟧ ("Isn't this the carpenter?"), the only place in the Gospels that calls Jesus himself a carpenter. Matthew has ⟦3⟧ ("the carpenter's son"). Luke, who moves the whole scene to the start of Jesus' ministry, has ⟦4⟧ ("Is this not Joseph's son?").

cites.words: οὐκ ἐδύνατο ἐκεῖ ποιῆσαι οὐδεμίαν δύναμιν

discoveries.title: The same miracle, at opposite ends

teaser.text: Luke's miraculous catch of fish happens at Peter's call. John's happens after the resurrection, and the nets behave differently.

body.text: Luke 5 and John 21 share a remarkable outline: a night of catching nothing, Jesus telling Peter where to cast, a catch too big to haul, and Peter's dramatic response. But they sit at opposite ends of the story, as the long ribbon across the map shows. Even the details answer each other. In Luke ⟦0⟧ ("their nets were beginning to tear"). In John, with 153 large fish, ⟦1⟧ ("the net was not torn"). Most scholars think one tradition lies behind both; the traditional reading is two separate catches, the second deliberately recalling the first. They disagree on whether it began as a call story that John turned into a resurrection appearance, or the reverse. Mark and Matthew give only the call itself, without the catch.

teaser.text: Matthew's best-known Beatitude has two words that Luke's does not.

body.text: Matthew: ⟦0⟧ ("Blessed are the poor *in spirit*"). Luke: ⟦1⟧ ("Blessed are the poor"). Luke's are addressed to "you" and are followed by matching woes against the rich, which Matthew lacks entirely. Matthew has nine Beatitudes to Luke's four, and his promise is "the kingdom of the heavens", his habitual phrase, where Luke has "the kingdom of God". Did Matthew spiritualize a saying about literal poverty, or did Luke sharpen a saying about humility into social reversal? Both answers have defenders, and many traditional readers think Jesus gave the blessings on two occasions, in two forms. The Greek shows that the same core sayings were shaped to fit each Gospel's emphasis.

mk.text: The shortest Gospel and, on most modern scholars' view, the earliest, written around 70 CE; the early church held that Matthew wrote first. Tradition, from Papias in the early 2nd century, credits it to John Mark, who recorded Peter's preaching. Mark's Greek is plain and fast: sentences strung together with ⟦0⟧ (“and immediately”), and vivid present tenses. It opens without a birth story, ⟦1⟧ (“the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ”); the SBLGNT omits “Son of God” here, following some early manuscripts. Mark's Jesus is urgent and secretive, his disciples persistently fail to understand, and the oldest manuscripts end at the empty tomb in fear. The vocabulary below shows the texture: *euthys*, unclean spirits, the sea, Jesus “looking around”.

mt.text: Tradition ascribes this Gospel to the apostle Matthew, the tax collector, and the early church placed it first. On the majority modern view it rewrites about 90% of Mark and adds a large body of teaching, gathered into five great discourses. Many readers see a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses. It begins with a genealogy, ⟦0⟧ (“the book of the genesis”), echoing Genesis itself, and keeps showing scripture fulfilled. Its Jesus comes ⟦1⟧ (“not to abolish but to fulfill”) the Law, and its closing promise, “I am with you always”, answers the Emmanuel of its first chapter, ⟦2⟧ (“God with us”). The vocabulary below shows Matthew's habits: *tote* (“then”), “the kingdom of **heaven**”, hypocrites, and the formal “came to him”.

lk.text: The only evangelist who explains his method, Luke writes in polished Greek for a patron, ⟦0⟧ (“most excellent Theophilus”), promising an account written ⟦1⟧ (“carefully, in order”). His Gospel is the first volume of a two-part work that continues in Acts. Tradition identifies him as Luke the physician, Paul's travelling companion. It is shaped by a journey toward Jerusalem, a word near the top of his vocabulary list, and by concern for the poor, women, Samaritans and sinners: ⟦2⟧ (“the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost”). Many of the best-loved parables, including the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, appear only in Luke.

cites.words: ἦλθεν γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ζητῆσαι καὶ σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός

jn.text: John is the Gospel that stands apart. It opens before creation, ⟦0⟧ (“in the beginning was the Word”), and announces that ⟦1⟧ (“the Word became flesh”). John has few parables and no exorcisms. In their place are long discourses, seven “signs”, and “I am” sayings, which is why *egō* (“I”) sits near the top of its vocabulary list, alongside “world”, “believe”, “Father”, “testify” and “remain”. It shares relatively little wording with the Synoptics, as this site's map shows. Tradition attributes it to John son of Zebedee, the “disciple whom Jesus loved”, writing late in life at Ephesus. It explains its own purpose: ⟦2⟧ (“these things are written so that you may believe”).
